speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, millions of Canadians over the last few hours have been watching with horror the results of yesterday's disastrous earthquake in California.
We realize that in the days and months that lie ahead Californians will be faced with a monumental clean up effort. We want those involved to know that they have the encouragement and support of all Canadians. Our sympathies lie with all Americans suffering as a result of this tragedy.
Through the Federal Emergency Management Agency, the President and the American Government were able to respond to this tragedy within a few minutes. This tragedy would have been even more devastating had it had not been for the established support systems and the thousands of ordinary and trained civilians prepared to respond quickly.
Mr. Speaker, today Canadians need some answers. What kind of emergency measures organization do we have? Do we have trained emergency personnel? Do we have strong municipal infrastructures?
Specifically, would we be able to respond to a disaster in any region of Canada with the same speed and expertise as the Americans have shown in the past few hours?

Mr. Speaker, 60 years ago today, on October 18, 1929, the women of Canada were formally recognized as persons by the British Privy Council. The Person's Case, as it has become to be known, is the chronicle of the efforts of five courageous Alberta women who persevered against a host of legal and social obstacles to win acknowledgement that Canadian women are indeed persons and are therefore eligible to be summoned to the Senate.
Last week six Canadians were honoured by our government for their dedication to the principles of equality and the individual's right to self-determination.
I congratulate this year's recipients: Kay Armstrong of Saanichton, British Columbia; the Honourable Ellen Fairclough of Hamilton; Dorothy Inglis of St. John's; Helen Levine of Ottawa; Alphonsine Par-Howlett of Westmount, Quebec; and Caroline Robins of Saskatoon.
Their efforts reinforce the significance and the relevance of the Person's Case as an important episode in Canadian history.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to call the attention of the House and the government to an effect that the VIA Rail cuts are having on a particular group of people, a group whose needs have not received that much attention in the entire debate about the VIA Rail cuts.
I am talking about people who have cottages on the CN main line from Winnipeg to Farlane. These are people who used to be served by a special train on the weekends through the summer and who some years ago had that service incorporated into the Winnipeg-Ca-preol line.
The service of the Winnipeg-Capreol line as a result of the government's proposals is now to be incorporated into the transcontinental service. Some remote communities like Rice Lake and Winnitoba have absolutely no road service whatsoever. The needs of these communities cannot be met in any other way except by a train that

October 18, 1989
stops at all those places and goes down at times when people normally want to go to their cottages.
The transcontinental train will not do that. It will leave on a Saturday night and come back on a Monday morning, which is totally useless.
Mr. Speaker, the forest fire that swept through that country a year ago was less of a threat to those peoples' investments than this government is proving to be.

Mr. Speaker, on October 18, 1929, the women of Canada obtained legal status as persons. Their long legal and political struggle opened the way for a host of initiatives to promote the status of women in Canada. One of these and perhaps the most important one was the appointment in 1970 of the Royal Commission of Inquiry on the Status of Women, which contributed toward achieving full equality of men and women in this country.
The federal Government's commitment at the time, which was to enable Canadian women to realize their ambitions and their full potential, is still appropriate today, and the Government fully subscribes to that commitment. It was in this perspective that the Government published a document entitled Dimensions of Equality, which appeared in 1986 and was subsequently reprinted. The document contains a federal work plan for women's equality. Mr. Speaker, the anniversary we are commemorating today must remain forever inscribed in the memory of all Canadians, as a tribute not only to our pioneers but also to all those women who proudly followed in their footsteps.

Mr. Speaker, democracy is not about singulars or plurals or contrived technicalities. It is about a principle and a belief in a
spirit that goes beyond partisan politics and personal agendas.
On Monday night 600,000 Albertans marched to the polls in the belief that Parliament must be fully democratic, not half democratic. It is no longer a matter of claiming to support democracy or claiming to support Senate reform. Senate reform has already begun. Either we in this House are fighting for it or we are fighting against it.
I urge the Prime Minister to join in this movement by confirming without delay Stan Waters' election to the Senate of Canada. This is a minimum test of his willingness to listen to Alberta. Other tests will come later as Albertans wait for action on the constitutional and fiscal policies on which they have sent a clear message.
Mr. Speaker, make no mistake. If the Prime Minister and his party ignore this election, they will make Mr. Waters a symbol and it will be my party that benefits. If they accept this election and act, Mr. Waters will be a senator and we all will gain.

Mr. Speaker, once again an idea that will revolutionize Confederation has come from the west. After decades of academic discussions and government reports, Senate reform is becoming a reality.
Whether this government will take heed of this fact or not is the only question left. Yesterday we saw in this House a government led by the famous Deputy Prime Minister from Alberta, in complete disarray. It is obvious it does not know what to do. While that is not a surprise it brings the issue of Senate reform into urgent focus.
The west has constitutional needs that must be addressed. We have been patient, but patience has not advanced the cause of Senate reform one bit.
Because of the success of the Alberta Senate election Manitoba is now considering using the election process to nominate senators. I am proud to say that the Liberal party in Manitoba has been on record for many years endorsing the Triple E Senate proposal. This govern-
October 18, 1989

ment should stop wondering what to do and accept the will of the Alberta electorate.
There is nothing more powerful than an idea whose time has come. Senate reform is here. It is happening whether the Conservative party wants it or not.

Mr. Speaker, independent car dealers from across Canada have established an excellent record of service to Canadian customers. In a business in which there is real competition, automobile dealers have served Canadian transportation needs by both selling and leasing cars to the satisfaction of their customers.
Over the past few years we have seen a quiet but persistent pressure from chartered banks in this country to allow them to enter the automobile leasing field. These banks wish to deal directly with customers for lease requirements. The pressures a large financial institution would place into the automobile leasing industry would have a negative effect and be totally unfair to the large investments dealers have made.
Banks must not be allowed to enter the automobile leasing business. I will continue to stand up for the car dealers across Canada and urge this House to oppose the intrusion into the car business by the banks of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to commemorate the sixtieth anniversary of the Person's Case; 60 years ago today women became persons under Canadian law. It is ironic that today the Conservative government is threatening to take away women's legal rights. A new law on abortion will open the floodgates to invasive legal cases such as the Daigle case. A new law will provide a basis for a series of court challenges just at the time when the Supreme Court is shutting down current legal avenues available.
We will once again see women dragged before the courts and publicly humiliated. In 1989 we are facing another legal equality crisis. Raising the legal status of the foetus over the legal rights of women to make decisions about our own bodies would be a giant step
backward for women's legal equality. Women will not be persons unless we have legal control over our own bodies and our own lives.

Mr. Speaker, today is a very special day for Chief Harry Chonkolay of the Dene Tha' Band in northwestern Alberta. Today Chief Chonkolay will be appointed to the Order of Canada to commemorate 50 years as chief of that band.
Harry Chonkolay was elected chief of the band on June 17,1938. During the 51 years he has served as chief, the band has seen many changes from its traditional way of life. He has given valuable and inspirational leadership to his people in their transition from a hunting and trapping society to one in step with modem times.
Chief Chonkolay has always stressed the importance of education and at the same time promoted the traditional values of his people, their language and their culture. He has served his people with integrity, dignity and dedication.
All one has to do is spend a few minutes with this man to recognize the wisdom and knowledge that he has obtained during his years as chief of the Dene Tha' Band.
This remarkable man is visiting us here today in the House of Commons.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, in 1986 the Department of the Environment wrote a pamphlet for public information entitled Storm Warning. It was suppressed by the then Minister of the Environment, Mr. McMillan, and the Minister of National Health and Welfare. When Storm Warning was finally released, its message was ignored.
Here is a sample of the message in Storm Warning:
Even the most careful person can be exposed to toxic substances
through the food chain.
In Storm Warning the various threats to health posed by toxic chemicals in the Great Lakes region are set out. Last week, three years later, the present minister of

October 18, 1989
Oral Questions
health announced that he wants a health study into toxic contamination in the Great Lakes region.
Instead of proceeding in 1986 to take preventive measures, three years later the government proceeds with a study which could delay action until its completion in 1994. When the health of Canadians is in danger, and despite earlier warnings, this government wasted three years before acting. What a sham.

Mr. Speaker, 60 years ago today, Canadian women won a major battle in their struggle to augment their political rights.
Today marks the anniversary of what is referred to as the person's case. Because of this historic ruling, Canadian women were legally recognized as persons. They also obtained the right to be appointed to the Senate.
Full political rights for women did not become a reality without a hard struggle by groups of Canadian women, and especially one particular group, later referred to as the Famous Five. They were: Emily Murphy, Nellie McClung, Louise McKinney, Irene Parlby and Henrietta Muir Edwards.
Thanks to their courage and determination, the lives of all Canadian women have been enriched.
As was the case with much of the history of Canadian women, the person's case was forgotten for 50 years. In honor of the Famous Five, the Persons Award was established in 1979 to acknowledge exceptional contributions toward improving the status of Canadian women.
Last week, the Governor General gave the Persons Award to six women whose commitment to defending the rights of women and improving the status of women has been a source of inspiration for us all.
On this anniversary, I ask you to join me-

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance.
The provincial Finance Ministers have declared that a new federal sales tax on top of their provincial taxes would be terribly complex and impossible to administer. The federal Minister of Finance has accused the provincial Ministers of indulging in petty politics. He said, and I quote: "I know better than they do what the effects of this tax will be". That was a very modest statement by our Finance Minister.
Mr. Speaker, in this connection, I would like to quote from a document entitled Sales Tax Reform, published under the authority of the Hon. Michael H. Wilson, Minister of Finance.
I quote at page 48: "Without a common base, little tax simplification would be possible-the system could become more complex-this layer of complexity would be compounded and spread across the country-if all governments were to have different tax bases, the system would be a national tax in name only. Effectively, it would be unworkable."
I mention this because it is exactly what the provincial Finance Ministers said yesterday.
How can the federal Minister accuse the provinces of petty politics when they are only repeating what he himself said in a document he tabled in the House of Commons?

Mr. Speaker, while I do not have that page 54 in front of me
here-

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader; Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
You wrote it.
October 18, 1989

-I think the quote the hon. member is referring to is that if you are going to have a national sales tax you have to have a common tax base, but the point of the matter is that my first choice had been a national sales tax. We have been working on that since early 1987 to try to achieve a national sales tax. Unfortunately that was not achievable.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader; Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Because you failed.

We have decided that we must go ahead. Because the existing federal sales tax on manufactured products is not working, as my friend I am sure would agree, we must change to a goods and services type of tax.
The point that I am making-and I have done this on many occasions-is that if the provinces want to come together and put forward a proposal that they can agree on, that the premiers agree on, we will talk with them.
Until they are off the wicket of simply opposing, simply saying that this tax is not good enough, this proposal is not good enough, without taking the responsibility of putting forward an alternative that we can talk about, there is nothing for us to meet and to talk about.

Mr. Speaker, the provincial ministers of finance were saying yesterday only what the minister in his document to Parliament had said quite categorically on June 19, 1987.
We have in this House, of course, a trade minister who has not read the trade deal. We have a fisheries minister who has not read the decision on salmon and herring. We now have the Minister of Finance who does not remember what he put in his document. I would be glad to let him have a copy so he can remember exactly what he said.

Pass the document over, John.
Oral Questions
Mr. Speaker, I can say parenthetically that no wonder we have a government that does not really worry about putting a 9 per cent tax on reading. None of them read.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I want to again quote the Minister of Finance from last night. He said that his counterparts, the provincial finance ministers, are "trying to cloud the issue so they could increase their own taxes". Those were his words.
Where does the man who has increased taxes in this country 31 times since he became minister, who is now trying to impose a 9 per cent tax on everything that moves, get off by telling the provincial ministers of finance that they are now trying to increase taxes?
Hear, hear!
Mr. Speaker, just in response to the cheap shot that the hon. member took-
Oh, oh!

-I have read that document precisely as I have read every other document that has been put out under my signature. When the hon. member reminds me of something that was put out two and one-half years ago, no, I do not remember every word of that.
The hon. member has raised a specific question about the provinces wanting to use this as a way of hiding their own intentions of raising taxes. That is very clear. They are making it quite clear that they want to raise taxes and they are going to use, they say, the GST as a reason for doing it. Mr. Speaker, I can be quite categoric. There will not be a reason for the provinces to raise their taxes based on the goods and services tax, based on the way they are raising taxes today.
We have been quite up front about raising taxes, but we have also been very up front about controlling government spending. We have a government spending record where we have increased government program spending by 3.6 per cent. No other province over the same five-year period has a spending record as good as that. The average of the provinces is a 6.4 per cent increase compared with our 3.6 per cent increase. The province of Ontario had a 9.5 per cent increase. This is

October 18, 1989
Oral Questions
an example of how well we are controlling spending on this side of the House.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, it is a flagrant example of the pot calling the kettle black. Tax up front? An invisible tax, secret from the consumers of Canada.
The Minister of Finance said last night, and I want to quote him again: "Provincial ministers of finance are trying to set themselves up to raise taxes, and they shouldn't do it". "They shouldn't do it", he says. Then in a pious way he said: "We all serve one taxpayer and they are trying to set up that one taxpayer so that they can increase taxes". Those were his words.
This man who is trying to make a tax grab in the amount of $29 billion, a larger tax grab than all the provincial income taxes put together, all the territorial taxes together, is accusing his provincial counterparts of a tax grab. This man who is going to force on the people of Newfoundland a total over-all sales tax rate of up to 26 per cent is saying that other people are trying to raise taxes.
If this Minister of Finance really believes that it is wrong for his provincial counterparts to raise taxes as he said last night, why is it not wrong for him to impose the largest tax grab in Canadian history? If they shouldn't do it, why should he do it?
Mr. Speaker, let me be quite categoric. This goods and services tax is replacing an existing tax.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader; Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Nonsense.
He says "nonsense", and he is saying that I have not read the document. Maybe he should read the document once or twice.
How about revenue neutral?

Would you like to just listen to the answer?
Some $24 billion dollars will be raised from this tax; $18.5 billion will be used to replace the revenues from the existing tax; $5.5 billion will be put back into the tax system through a goods and services tax credit, through the reduction in the middle income tax rate, and through
the automatic indexing that is required under the terms of existing Canadian law, so it is not the tax grab that the hon. member refers to.
The point that I was making is that for the provinces to use the goods and services tax as an excuse for raising their taxes is unwarranted, because there will not be a reason based on the goods and services tax for them to increase their taxes. They should not use that as a basis for them to raise their own taxes.
The other misinformation the right hon. leader of the opposition is using is to say that Newfoundland will have to go to a 26 per cent sales tax. That is nonsense. There is categorically no reason absolutely whatsoever. If Mr. Kitchen wants to discuss that with me, I would suggest he give me a phone call and find out the true facts as to what the impact of the sales tax will be before he makes those unwarranted statements.

Mr. Speaker, today the situation is as honeless as ever. The Minister of Finance is trying to tell us that he is right and everybody else is wrong. Yesterday, the provinces said: "Unacceptable". They will have no part of it. I want to ask the Minister of Finance, who supposedly is part of a government of national reconciliation and is now about to carry off a unilateral coup unique in Canada's history and in our tax system, what justification he has for introducing this tax, when all provincial ministers are telling him they want no part of it and when the Canadian public says he is wrong? Who supports the Ministerof Finance, aside from a few backbenchers who won't listen to their constituents?

Mr. Speaker, I want to make it absolutely clear that there is no basis for the provinces to raise their taxes. That is quite clear, if they use the GST as an excuse to raise their own taxes.
Now the hon. member is saying: "Are we doing something unilateral"? We spent two years of consultations with officials, with the ministers, talking about a proposed national sales tax. The provinces do not want that national sales tax. It is quite clear from the display of comments that we heard at the premiers' meeting in
October 18, 1989

August and at the finance ministers' meeting yesterday that the provinces do not want to participate.
The federal government must move ahead, because all sides of this House agree, and if hon. members opposite have forgotten, Liberals and New Democrats signed the finance Committee report twice in the last Parliament saying that we have to move to a new sales tax. I will remind the member from Ottawa-Vanier of his comments. We must move to this tax. The provinces do not have to move to the tax. That is why we have to move ahead, and the provinces know that.

Mr. Speaker, there is a consensus at least on one thing among Canadians, among all provincial Ministers and all members on this side of the House, and that is that the Minister of Finance didn't do his homework. Canadians want taxes that are visible, neutral and fair. Unfortunately, the proposals presented by the Minister of Finance do not pass that test. Consequently, I would ask the Minister of Finance, considering the unanimous rejection of his proposals, whether he has the courage to withdraw them immediately.

Mr. Speaker, the answer is no. We have put forward a technical paper for further consultation. The finance committee is holding hearings right now. We are having consultations with various groups that want to meet with us to see whether there are ways of improving the document. But for him to suggest that we are going to withdraw this, I say to the leader of the Liberal party, where are you on this debate?
Oh, oh!
Oh, yes, they say: We are against it. But ask us to put up an alternative? Oh, no, we would not sully our hands by putting up an alternative. All we are going to do is-
Hear, hear!
I say to the Leader of the Opposition, get into the ballgame. Put some facts on the table and quit just opposing.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance has made a statement that not only
Oral Questions
would the provincial treasurers, without exception, disagree with but all Canadians who have been following this tax debate, except his own back-benchers, will disagree with it.
He has just said that provinces do not have to worry about a negative impact because of this tax. He knows that this reduction in income tax that he has just alluded to is going to cost the provinces. The impact on inflation is going to cost the provinces. Allowing for some increases in wages and salaries related to inflation is going to cost the provinces.
According to figures that have been produced, Manitoba claims it will cost it $70 million, New Brunswick $145 million, Newfoundland $85 million. We heard from the Minister of Finance for Newfoundland today, saying that the only way he could cope with it is to cut services in an already poor province, or increase taxes. He said it is going to go up to a net effect of a 25 per cent sales tax.
I want to ask the Minister of Finance why he is putting this unfair burden particularly on the poorer provinces of Canada?

Mr. Speaker, there is no unfair burden being put upon poorer provinces of this country. As I have said before and I will repeat again, they will not be negatively affected by the introduction of a goods and services tax.
Further to that, the poorer provinces of the country, because they have proportionately more low-income people, will get a greater share of the goods and services tax credit. That works out to $275 per adult, $100 per child, and it works out for residents over-all to $170 per capita in the GST credit. The province of Newfoundland will be a proportionately greater recipient of that than say the province of Ontario.

Mr. Speaker, I do not need to remind the Minister of Finance, but I will. This government has already, in terms of the poorer provinces, cut back on regional development programs, cut back on health transfer payments, cut back on VIA Rail, which is particularly bad for the lower income provinces, and now a GST impact that he has not denied. I challenge him to produce his own figures. Because of its impact on inflation, because of the income tax change, he is hitting the provinces again. If you consider almost every aspect of this government's policy, including the GST, it is the

Oral Questions
poorest provinces in Canada that are getting it in the neck, and I want the Minister of Finance to justify that.

Mr. Speaker, it is hard to justify something that is not happening. I have said that the poorer provinces will be proportionately greater beneficiaries of the goods and services tax credit. Equalization payments during our term of office have increased a good deal faster than the rate of growth of normal federal-provincial transfers.
The poorer provinces of this country receive 40 per cent to 55 per cent of their revenues, depending on the province, directly from the Government of Canada. That is something that clearly demonstrates the ongoing support which this government has for the poorer provinces of this country.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance suggested a few minutes ago that this new sales tax would have no negative impact on the provinces, specifically the poor provinces. He said so, but everyone else says the opposite! Not only the Opposition but all the provinces and experts outside the Government!
If the finance minister does not agree, would he give the House of Commons the figures which tell a different story? That is the challenge I make to the Minister of Finance.

Mr. Wilson (Etobicoke Centre) Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is using figures I have not seen. I presume, from what he has said, that they have just been released. I am going to have a look at those figures and I will be in a position to comment on them after I have seen how the provinces have developed those figures.
It is clear in the economic analysis that has been done by the Government of Canada that the Atlantic provinces, the prairie provinces and British Columbia have an economic benefit. The economic impact is greater for them than for the national average, but all provinces, including the provinces of Quebec and Ontario, benefit from the introduction of this tax, but it is the provinces that are farther away from central Canada that have the greatest proportion of benefit.

Mr. Francis G. LeBIanc (Cape Breton Highlands-
Canso): Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Fisheries. Yesterday the minister told the House that his government would wait 30 days before announcing whether it will accept Monday's free trade panel ruling on landing requirements for west coast salmon and herring. Yet in his press release he declared that the panel accepted the legitimacy of Canada's position on the use of these landing requirements, even though the panel obliges Canada to permit over-the-side sales of unprocessed fish, something which the landing requirements were put in place to prevent.
If the minister considers this sell-out a victory for Canada, why is he now saying he will take 30 days to review the decision? Otherwise, will he stand up now for Canadian jobs and reject this ruling?
Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Fisheries and
Oceans): Mr. Speaker, it happens to be the opposition members who have been using the term "victory" to describe this panel finding. In fact, if the hon. member and his leader would read the finding-because I think perhaps they could use some reading lessons-they would learn that in no less than 10 places in this document, Canada's sovereignty under Canadian fisheries legislation is fully accepted as the primary means of managing and conserving our fishery stocks, which is precisely what I said yesterday.

My
supplementary question is for the same minister. So it is not a victory. We are clear about that.
How does the minister reconcile this answer with statements by the government leader in the Senate that, "the government accepts the finding and intends to work within the context of that finding", and by U.S. trade representative Carla Hills, who said yesterday, "We fully expect Canada will promptly comply with the panel ruling"? Who speaks for the government on this issue? Is it the minister of fisheries, is it the Senate government leader, or is it Carla Hills?

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member should know that it is the Government of Canada that speaks for Canada on this issue. The government received this panel report on Monday. Under the Free Trade Agree-
October 18, 1989

ment, there is provision to review it and analyse it over a 30-day period before taking a position.
If the hon. member will check the transcripts of the government Leader in the Senate, I believe he will find that the government leader in the other place will be clarifying his statement and correcting it because the government has not yet decided what position will be taken in the disposition of this report.

Mr. Speaker, the minister of fisheries must be a slow reader if it takes 30 days.
Yesterday the minister told this House the panel finding "clearly recognizes Canada's right to management of fish stocks-, in accordance with our sovereign rights". What he does not say is that those rights extend only as far as the United States permits.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: You're reading, Coline.

Yes, Mr. Speaker, one has to read because one wants to remember what is being said in this House. The Minister of Finance sometimes forgets.
On the west coast, you have the U.S. telling us that our conservation for herring and salmon is a restrictive trade. On the east coast, the U.S. is passing legislation to conserve its lobster fishery against our own lobster fishing industries.

Mr. Speaker, here we have another member of the opposition who does not read. If the hon. member would search her memory channels she would learn that it was the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade talks which decided that our old processing regulations were discriminatory in that they wanted special treatment for the Canadian industry that was denied the American industry. Because we export 80 per cent of the fish, particularly that from her own constituency, to the United States, we have to play by those rules. But I must say that this panel finding, the consensus of a panel on which three Canadians sit, suggests that the sovereignty

of Canada's right to manage and conserve the fishery stocks of Canada takes precedence over all other considerations.

Mr. Speaker, the minister does not understand. We have agreed, we have a sovereign right to our natural resources. Surely free trade did not take that away from us.
I am saying that that minister does not understand that there are no countermeasures for what they are telling us is a restrictive trade. In the lobster area, the impending legislation before the U.S. government is going to be a restrictive trade.
What countermeasures, aside from diplomatic talks, is the minister going to present to the U.S. to protect the many thousands of lobster fishermen who begin their season with a complicated free trade agreement which has no countermeasures for us to resolve that dispute?
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member should know, and if she does not, perhaps she should pick up a newspaper and read, that the-
How condescending. What a pompous approach.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for South West Nova knows full well that there is proposed legislation before the U.S. Congress and House which would extend, in an extra-territorial fashion, United States conservation considerations and make them applicable to Canadian lobsters being exported to the United States. The hon. member knows that Canada has strongly protested any such proposed legislation because it would intrude upon our sovereignty to manage our lobster fishery according to our criteria, and it would violate in fact the principle of the free trade agreement.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. Yesterday, the minister touted Canada's great success in that the free trade panel, he claims, upholds Canada's sovereign right to control our own resource as long as we let the Americans tell us how many of our fish we can land.

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, certainly I am absolutely confident that we can do that because that is my responsibility under Canadian fisheries legislation.
Oh, oh!

In fact, Mr. Speaker, we still have about 27 days to carefully read this report. If the hon. member would read paragraph 7.40, for example, he would find that the Canadian prerogative takes proportion over any percentage of fish which might be accessed by sea by the Americans in that it it says, and I quote: "Though any such proportion would have to be determined on the basis of the actual data and management needs of each fishery or group of related fisheries, the panel was of the view that the 10 to 20 per cent range referred to earlier could provide appropriate guidance". speakeroldname: Hon. Bill McKnight (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think all members of the House would want to express sympathy to the families of those people in northern California who lost their lives, as well as to the other families who are there.
With regard to the hon. member's question, throughout government we have taken efforts to constrain spending and to bring about a rational approach to spending by the departments, particularly the departments to which the member refers.
With respect to emergency preparedness, I can inform the hon. member that next week, Tbesday through Thursday, in co-operation with the Government of British Columbia, there will be an emergency preparedness symposium held in British Columbia. I see the leader of the New Democratic Party laughing, Mr. Speaker. I would suggest that he knows, and his colleagues know, that the municipal and provincial governments have lead roles in emergency preparedness. They are the first on the ground. They are the first to react. We co-operate with them as a national government. We provide the expertise that we can provide. We have a training program and provinces have training programs. Located just some 30 miles from where the hon. member sits is one of the best emergency preparedness training programs for municipal and provincial bodies at Am-prior, supported by Emergency Preparedness Canada.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Employment and Immigration. For over 200 years, German speaking people have emigrated to Canada, making them the third largest ethnic and language group in Canada behind the English and French. In view of recent events with the thousands of people leaving East Germany and that many Canadians of German origin are anxious and willing to help some of these people come to Canada, is the Govern-

ment of Canada prepared to open our doors to some of these East German refugees?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think that all of us in this House have been touched by what we have seen in East Germany in recent weeks and months.
My officials and I have been in contact with the representatives of the German Canadian community. I will be meeting with the German Canadian Congress on October 26 and we will be discussing with them how the German Canadian community might assist with East Germans who may want to come to Canada.

Mr. Speaker, my question today is for the Minister of Justice.
As he knows, last week, at least 500 elected municipal officials met in Montreal at an international conference to discuss crime prevention. They raised the idea that prevention is at least as important as repression.
At the end of the conference, they issued a statement criticizing the federal government both for its lack of support for prevention projects and for its lack of leadership.
I ask the Minister of Justice how he will answer. [English]

speakeroldname: Hon. Doug Lewis (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate my colleague's comments. I was at the very same conference.
The federal government has been very actively involved in crime prevention. We are conducting surveys and studies. We are getting information on crime prevention policies and comparing these with the ones that exist in Europe, Australia and the United States. We were an active partner in the planning of the very conference that my friend was at.
We have provided the national drug strategy, the proceeds of crime legislation. All of these are part of an
Oral Questions
ongoing program of crime prevention which we think, according to the latest statistics, is succeeding.

Mr. Speaker, despite the Minister's statement, as he must know, the Canadians who were at the conference saw that the federal Government's participation was much less than that of other countries, especially from Europe.
I want to ask the Minister, since the Government transferred responsibility for prevention from the Solicitor General to Justice without transferring any funding, why not increase the funding, restore the funding that the Solicitor General had for prevention, instead of transferring responsibilities with no transfer of funding.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I reject that categorically. We organized the convention. We had most of the displays there from Health and Welfare and Solicitor General. The Solicitor General and I were both there and participated in the program. There was hardly any participation or displays from the municipalities. We were there. We were there in spades.

Mr. Speaker, for an investment of $10 million a year, the Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety has provided cost-free, unbiased, impartial information for a decade, and in the process, has saved the Government of Canada hundreds of millions of dollars a year in health care costs. Certainly what we are dealing with here is an ounce of prevention for a pound of cure. In fact, it is a good business practice.
My question is for the Minister of Labour. Why is this government gambling with a good investment of Canadian taxpayers' dollars?

Mr. Speaker, I would like to answer the hon. member that the Government of Canada takes no chances with the wonderful work done over the years by the Centre for Occupational Health and Safety. A while ago, in accordance with the director of the centre, we asked that a plan for financing the centre from non-government sources be drawn up, since the government has invested $60 million in this centre over the last 10 years. And I am

Oral Questions
very pleased to tell the hon. member opposite that about two weeks ago, the Board of the Centre rejected as inapplicable the plan submitted to it by the Director and asked a task force from the centre to prepare another plan to present to the Minister of Labour for meeting the objective we set for the Centre, namely to continue its excellent work but with funds from sources outside the federal treasury.

Mr. Speaker, I heard the minister say, "absolutely no risk", and yet this occupational health and safety centre, internationally recognized, has been built on trust between government, business and labour, and under a deal where they are going to find financing privately, labour has threatened to withdraw its service. There is risk, I want to remind the minister.
Given that for a decade, the Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety has paid for itself hundreds of times over, and given the potential of increased health care costs and losses in productivity, will the minister reinstate funding and admit that he has made a mistake?

Mr. Speaker, there is absolutely no risk that the centre will be closed because there are ample opportunities for the centre to find financing in the market-place. There are all kinds of avenues that have been considered by the council of governors and the proof of the pudding is in the fact that they have agreed to prepare a plan themselves to present to the Minister of Labour indicating that the plan can find the financing from other than the treasury of the federal government.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday, child care workers in Manitoba staged a day of protest outlining their anger at their status under the Tory government of that province.
Today is Person's Day, and is significant in that a woman's status and equality are very much dependent on her economic freedoms. Economic freedoms depend on the availability of safe, quality, affordable child care.
Would the Minister of Finance acknowledge that the Status of Women depends on the federal government and take the lead in supporting child care by providing adequate funding?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member well knows, the federal government shares in the funding of child care through the Canada Assistance Plan, an open-ended plan that the provinces can take up as they see fit. We are always there with them in providing that operating funding.
Having said that, we did have child care legislation in this Chamber. It was held up in the other place and did not pass. Since that time, the Prime Minister, the Minister of Health and Welfare and I have all been working very hard in assuring Canadians that we will have new child care legislation in this country. But I would encourage the provinces, in the meantime, to use the Canada Assistance Plan.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the hon. Minister of Employment and Immigration. In view of the fact that she now speaks on behalf of the Minister of Finance, possibly on this 60th anniversary of Person's Day, a day that is important to both of us as women, the minister responsible for the Status of Women might be prepared to finally go on the record in cabinet and publicly in support of additional funding for much needed child care.

speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think that every member in this House knows how much I care about this issue, whether it is Person's Day or not. As a member of this government, I can say we worked very hard on the legislation the last time. I was very proud of that legislation. If we had not run into problems in the other place from those people, we would have child care in place in Canada today.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. The minister is well aware of the serious situation concerning the huge increase in lamprey eels in the Great Lakes. I contacted him, and I know of others who have also contacted him. It is serious as far as the tourist industry, the sports fishing and commercial fishing industries are concerned.
I am wondering if the minister has been able to get any funds to look after this very serious situation.

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the members of the House will be pleased to learn that Canada is increasing substantially its contribution to the work of the Great Lakes Fisheries Commission. The Great Lakes Fisheries Commission was created in 1955 because of the heavy decimation of the Great Lakes fish stocks by the sea lamprey. I am pleased to report that the work of the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka and other members from the Great Lakes area in all parts of this House have enabled us to make this very important contribution to a very worthy program.

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I appreciate the unanimous consent for me to make a statement this afternoon.
I want to point out that the decision to increase planned immigration to Canada in 1990 from 165,000 to
175,000	immigrants as per the reports I tabled, an increase of 15,000 over the previous year's planning range, is a decision that is in keeping with the blueprint outlined in the Speech from the Throne.
The 1990 level was determined after consultations with provincial and territorial governments, as well as with non- governmental organizations, and represents a consensus which has emerged during our consultation process of the past several years.

The immigration levels this government has established, Madam Speaker, reflect a constantly evolving balance among many elements-family reunification, protection of genuine refugees, as well as labour market needs. All of these factors must be carefully weighed before we determine what level is best for Canada and the people who settle here.
We are now about to begin a series of consultations with government and service organizations to establish a longer-term plan for immigration levels and the balance among all of these categories.
Family reunification remains the cornerstone of the current immigration program and in 1990 Canada plans to admit 61,000 immigrants with close relatives in Canada-spouses, unmarried dependents and older parents.

This is 4,000 more than the 1989 target and reflects the expected demand of sponsorships for relatives of people now living in Canada under the expansion to the family class that we had introduced earlier.
Also in 1990 about 13,000 refugees will be admitted from abroad under government sponsorship. Within this

October 18, 1989
Statements by Ministers
global target the number accepted from Southeast Asia puts us on track to meeting the commitment that I announced in Geneva this summer to resettle 16,000 Southeast Asian refugees by 1992.
In 1990 we expect the private sector will sponsor the admission of some 13,000 refugees also as a continued expression of its commitment. In all, Canada will resettle some 26,000 refugees during 1990. Another 7,000 people are expected to be landed as refugees during 1990 after having been examined under our new refugee determination system.
Finally, 3,000 to 6,000 people with family ties to Canada will be admitted under special humanitarian measures.

These increased immigration figures reflect a broad consensus that emerged through consultations among national non-governmental organizations and regional, local and community groups over the past few years.
As all members of this House are aware, our immigration levels have increased every year since this government came into office. Immigration is currently around the post-war annual average.
But Canada needs to plan its immigration levels for more than a single year at a time, since levels decisions have an impact on many federal and provincial government departments as well as on agencies that help immigrants settle in Canada.
It is now time to re-evaluate the situation and prepare a comprehensive plan for the 1991-1995 period.

In preparing this plan, we will ask our consultative partners to take into consideration demographic movements, Canada's current and projected population size, where people choose to live, and related social and economic trends. The motivation behind the extensive consultations that I am launching in November 1989 is to continue to March 1990.
In expanding our consultations we will draw on a wider range of views in formulating immigration policy for the medium term. I intend to be personally involved in these consultations, because I want to emphasize that I attach considerable importance to this exercise.
We will ask experts on economic, social and demographic trends in immigration to contribute up to date information and data to our discussions. We will invite representatives from all levels of government, as well as from business, labour, health, social services and education, to make their views known in a series of multi-disciplinary dialogues.
One of the objectives of these consultations is to dispel myths about the effects that immigration has on Canada and to develop a broader dialogue on immigration.

I am sure that this dialogue will convince us even more that immigrants make a valuable contribution to Canada, that they enrich our society and our economy and that they help us maintain our tradition of tolerance which is envied by all.

I am confident that this exchange of views and information will assist the government in formulating the specific number and mix of immigrants that Canada should plan to admit during the 1991-1995 period in accordance with the government's general intention to increase immigration levels. I am looking forward to a constructive dialogue on the impacts of immigration, an important component of the economic and social development of our country.

Madam Speaker, I am very pleased on behalf of my colleague, the associate critic on immigration, the member of Parliament for Scarborough West, and my colleagues in the Liberal party to respond to what in essence was a very poor, unimaginative and uncreative blueprint if one can call it that. I say that for four reasons.
First, the increase in the announced levels for next year is only marginal and substantial at the very best. Not only does it keep with the past increases-for instance, last year it was 25,000-but it loses its impact particularly at a time when all the so-called experts are calling for an additional number of immigrants into Canada, and a substantial number.
Therefore it does not address the world realities or the needs of Canada because we have an ageing population and a dwindling birth rate. We have an out-migration of some 70,000 people a year and therefore we need to constructively and positively harness energies and engage Canadians in a debate on how we face this looming
October 18, 1989

crisis of population and population decline in this country.
We do not need a short-term five-year plan. What we need is long-term vision that will try to harness the viewpoints of all Canadians. What I would suggest to the minister is to appoint a royal commission so that it may once and for all try to tap into the views and the feelings of all Canadians, of all Canadian groups and entities from all regions of this country; so that we may look at immigration positively as opposed to leaving the important decisions for the year 2000, only to be faced with insurmountable challenges at that particular time which will only perhaps incite some kind of backlash across this country.
The second problem with these announced immigration levels is the issue of family class within the Tory agenda of immigration. Under successive Liberal governments the family class and assisted family class levels comprised approximately 50 per cent of our over-all immigration policy. It was clearly a cornerstone of Liberal immigration policy.
Under five successive years of Tory administration, we have seen the family class levels slip. Last year it was at 32 per cent; this year it is at 36 per cent. Business as usual.
What we are seeing is that the difference between the traditional levels of 50 per cent and some mid-30 range is causing a great deal of frustration among the many Canadian families we meet every week in our constituency offices, because they cannot sponsor quickly enough or successfully enough family reunification programs.
Therefore I reiterate that the Tories have failed to upgrade the family class level to its proper and traditional place, something that Canadians from coast to coast have been articulating and have been asking this government to do.
The third area is on the question of refugees. We have seen from our own documents that private sponsorship in the last number of years has doubled. It has gone from
6,000	a couple of years ago to 10,000 this year to 13,000 next year. At the same time, we have seen government levels stay the same. They have basically been the status quo.
Statements by Ministers
What we are seeing, of course, is a shift away from a strong government commitment to one of a greater community commitment. While the community commitment ought to be there, we are also saying that the government commitment should increase proportionately, because otherwise there would simply be a one-sided commitment and what we need is a two-prong approach.
Another matter dealing with refugees was the curious aspect that neither in the minister's response nor in her documents does she talk about the refugee backlog, which is an absolute mess and nightmare from the word go. There are over 100,000 people in the backlog, some
85,000	claimants all told. Up until a couple of weeks ago only 57 claims had been finally processed. Those people cannot afford to wait two, three or four years for that backlog to be cleared. Canada cannot afford to go through this expensive and time consuming exercise. What we need is a minister to recognize that there is a grey area between her black and white view of immigration, that there is a compromise solution that offers a win-win solution.
The fourth item is that this blueprint ignores the international realities and world opinion. For instance, the Prime Minister travelled to Singapore just a few days ago and he was criticized, justifiably so, for promoting a very selective immigration policy in that part of the world that "skimmed the cream", that allowed rich business immigrants to immigrate without balancing with family class, without balancing with refugees from that part of the world. The minister did not address this feature. She failed to address the other feature of business immigration, that is say, to ensure that the business proposals by which they are approved are in fact being realized in this country.
On the international stage the minister also failed to make any mention about the historical developments in eastern Europe, particularly the question of East German migration and particularly since she has had discussions with the Canadian German community in this country. We allowed special movements in 1956 from Hungary of 37,000; in 1968,12,000 Czechoslovakians; and in 1982, 10,000 Polish citizens. There is not one mention about Canada being in touch with the movements in eastern Europe vis-a-vis immigration.
Finally, I also would like to simply and quickly address a comment made by the Prime Minister whereby he suggested that there are ''racist tendencies" in some Canadians about refugees and immigration. This is the same Prime Minister who announced a national crisis and called a national emergency session of Parliament

October 18, 1989
Statements by Ministers
over a couple of hundred refugee claimants who landed in eastern Canada. That lecture is misguided and, if there is any tolerance, understanding, or education, it ought to start with the Prime Minister and the government.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity and I thank the House for agreeing to make it possible for the statement and the replies, because the minister's report shows a consistently anti-democratic bias throughout.
She restricted both the total increase in immigration and the annual consultation, while the government cuts back on adjustment programs for immigrants. She is restricting family reunification as a proportion, while expanding the brain drain. She restricts refugees from police states and death squads in Central America so as to increase economic migrants from eastern Europe.
In Canada, the minister is sweeping nearly 100,000 refugee claimants of the old backlog under the rug by denying them right of counsel and using specially distorted guidelines for so-called humanitarian review. Furthermore, she refuses to say what she will do with the 7,500 in the new refugee backlog for 1989.
The increase of only 10,000 or 15,000 total immigration flies against the unanimous recommendations of the Tory led committee on labour, employment and immigration in 1985. Holding back the demographic study that was promised for 1988 and excluding many immigrant support groups from the consultation enables her to run her program through with sham consultation.
While her colleagues reduce opportunities for immigrants, especially women, to learn English or French as a second language, by cancelling the citizenship instruction and language training program she cuts back job training opportunities for immigrants as well as Canadian born workers.
While increasing the target for family reunification, which is the cornerstone of her immigration policy, by only 7 per cent, she boosts the business immigrants and families of selected workers by 21 per cent and the retirees by 50 per cent. This goes with increasing delays
in family class applications as immigration staff is transferred to business immigration.
The anti-democratic bias shows most in the minister's overseas refugee plan. She is increasing the level for eastern Europe and reducing the level for Latin America. She hides almost 4,000 questionable refugees from eastern Europe by not including them in her totals. They are the designated class who need not show a well-founded fear of persecution. Yet, eastern Europe is becoming more free, as she herself acknowledges, while the death squad killings increase in Guatemala, El Salvador and Chile. She claims that private sponsorships for Central America have declined, although she knows that the reason why sponsorships have declined is that her overseas consular officers have delayed interviews and applications.
Finally, the Minister predicts only 7,000 to be landed annually of those who claim refugee status while in Canada since January 1, 1989. This is shocking. After more than nine months the immigration and refugee board has already granted refugee status to 3,049, while 7,555 have not yet received decisions in their cases. Most of them have not even had their cases opened. So does the Minister plan to deport over 4,500 of them and any more that come before December 31, without giving them any hearing at all on their claims?

Madam Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to take part in this debate and to speak in support of this important and timely bill.
In my remarks this afternoon I want to direct the attention of the House to an examination of the package of measures in Bill C-28 as a whole. Indeed, I would like to look at the bill in the context of our budgetary and economic policy as a whole. In that context, I want to affirm that the policy set out in this bill is a reasonable one, a fair one and, not least, a necessary one.
When I say the measures in this bill are reasonable, I mean they are appropriate to the economic circumstances we are in. We are in a serious situation, particularly with respect to the growing public debt, and the measures that address the problem. To demonstrate what I mean, let us examine just two of them: first, the surtaxes. I believe it is reasonable to expect all taxpayers to bear some of the burden of deficit reduction, since the deficit is a problem that affects everyone. That is why we have proposed to increase the federal surtax by 2 percentage points, from 3 per cent to 5 per cent, effective July 1, 1989.

October 18, 1989
Government Orders
The new high income surtax of 3 per cent will be levied on people with incomes over $70,000. In addition to the general surtax this will ensure that the burden of deficit reduction falls most heavily on those who are best able to carry it.
Second, the large corporations tax. I believe it is reasonable to expect all large corporations in Canada to pay a fair share of federal tax and thus help contribute to the deficit reduction effort. This new tax will only apply on capital in excess of $10 million and thus smaller businesses are not subject to this tax. The budget papers show that about 3,600 large corporations, accounting for approximately three-quarters of the total corporate capital employed in Canada, will be subject to this tax.
I am satisfied that when this bill is examined in committee, the members of the committee will find that the policy it implements is a reasonable one like the two specific provisions I have just noted.
My second concern and a constant concern of the government is with fairness. We want to ensure that the impact of our policies will place the greater burden on those who are better able to cany it, and we want to ensure that everyone who is able is helping solve our common problems. A number of the measures in this bill contribute to the fairness of the package. The two measures I have just mentioned, for example, ensure that those with higher incomes do contribute a fair share.
Other measures demonstrate the government's commitment to targeting assistance to those who need it most. To increase the fairness of the system we are targeting more assistance to lower-income Canadians by doubling the refundable sales tax credits for adults and children and by raising the income threshold so more people will qualify for the full credit. For those who receive the full credit, these measures will more than compensate for the federal sales tax increases that were announced in the April budget.
A second example of a measure designed to increase the fairness of the income tax system is our proposal to ensure that Canadians with incomes over $50,000 a year repay the benefits received under the family allowance and the old age security programs. The proposal respects the principle of universality in social programs, which
this government fully accepts, by ensuring that all eligible persons continue to receive these payments.
The programs remain untouched because the amount of repayment does not depend on the status of the individual but on his or her income and is administered through the personal income tax system. Of course these benefits are already subject to personal income tax and, therefore, are already being partially repaid at progressive rates by all taxpayers. Lower and middle income Canadians who receive these benefits will not be affected by this measure, and those whose incomes drop below the threshold will continue to enjoy full benefits. The $50,000 threshold is indexed on the same basis as other indexed brackets and thresholds in the tax system. As well, the level of the threshold will be reviewed periodically and adjusted as appropriate.
Other measures also improve the fairness of the system. I want to draw attention to the new deductions in respect of part-time attendant care for the working disabled and to the new drought relief tax deferral for cattle farmers who have had to reduce the size of then-breeding herds because of the drought. These provisions are designed to assist those with special needs and will continue to enhance the over-all fairness of the tax system.
To have a fair tax system we must have a fair tax base. Therefore a number of measures are included in this bill to make the tax base more equitable. An example is our proposal to tax accrued investment income on an annual basis. This will help ensure that those who invest in contracts and pay income annually and those who choose to invest in compound instruments will be taxed on a comparable basis.
Measures relating to the taxation of leasing profits will ensure that the leasing industry bears its fair share of tax and will help curtail the use of leasing as an after tax financing mechanism. At the same time we were careful to ensure that these proposals will not interfere with the legitimate use of leasing.
Finally, I want to draw attention to a third characteristic of the measures in this bill. I believe they are reasonable and they make the system more fair. They are also necessary. They accept the reality of constraints imposed by a growing public debt and demonstrate that this government is acting effectively to face the many challenges that we face as a result. The debt is large, and is growing as we speak. By this time tomorrow the debt
October 18, 1989

will be larger by more than $80 million. Two weeks from now it will have grown by another $1 billion.
The main reason for this dramatic rate of growth is that the interest payments on the debt are increasing rapidly. Only 20 years ago, just 12 cents of every dollar taxpayers sent to Ottawa went to interest payments. By 1984, that figure had already grown to 32 cents, and this year it is over 35 cents.
The debt is a major obstacle to building the kind of future we want for ourselves and for our children. But this does not have to happen. This does not have to be the legacy by which future generations of Canadians remember us. We can and we must stop borrowing from our children and their futures. We must all realize that it is too easy to borrow from future generations. They cannot speak in this debate. They are not here to vote on this legislation. But they are the ones who would face the consequences if we did not act. So we, in this House-all of its members-must speak for them. We must act on their behalf by taking the necessary actions now to reduce the deficit and control the growth of the debt. We must start paying our own way.
This is exactly what our government has been trying to do from the first day that we took office. From day one we recognized how serious the debt problem really was and we have been acting responsibly to bring it under control.
In this budget, which this bill will help implement, the Minister of Finance proved he is not complacent. He introduced a careful balance of expenditure and revenue measures to deal with the debt. These debt control measures will cut more than $5 billion from the projected deficit this year and $9 billion next year. The budget measures will cut the annual deficit in half, to $15 billion by the year 1993-94. These are reasonable measures. They are fair measures and they are necessary measures which recognize that deficit reduction has a greater purpose. It provides more flexibility for the government to ensure that the programs Canadians value can be maintained; it means that Canadians have greater confidence in their economy and their future; it holds out on the promise of sustained economic growth, improved competitiveness and the creation of productive
Government Orders
jobs; and it is an essential pre-condition for an increasing prosperous and compassionate Canada.
In summary, Madam Speaker, I believe the measures in Bill C-28 are an integral part of the reasonable, fair and necessary economic policy set out by this government at the beginning of its term in office which we have followed consistently since that time.

Madam Speaker, I think rubbish and nonsense are euphemisms for pure unadulterated garbage. The member did not mention the word clawback. I believe it was invented by the Conservative government and it is a very appropriate term. She should have noted that $50,000 now will certainly not be $50,000 in five years, ten years and 20 years. Does the hon. member agree with the finance committee chairman's statement that this is a pernicious, sneaky attack on universality? It is the end of universality as we know it. Does she not accept the fact that it will affect several thousand seniors now but as many as one million in 20 years from now? Does she not agree that this is effectively the end of universality as we know it?

Madam Speaker, maybe the gentleman does know what rubbish is all about, but when I speak I am sincere in saying that what this government is doing is necessary to protect our seniors now and in the future. Universality is not being threatened.
As I stated in my speech, old age security payments are in place. They will stay in place when seniors receive their cheque every month. They can spend that. There is no limit as far as whether they have to return so much on a certain month. We will be dealing with this in the income tax legislation, as we have done with all other issues, to ensure that seniors in the future do receive what is necessary for a good living.

Madam Speaker, the speech just given by the hon. member for Wild Rose was absolutely incredible. In the course of her statement she indicated that this government had concentrated its efforts on deficit reduction.
Would she not agree with me that this government is obviously a colossal flop when it comes to deficit reduction? The Minister of Finance in his first budget in 1984 indicated that the deficit this financial year would be $16 billion dollars and it is $30 billion. Also he indicated that he was going to reduce the deficit and, in fact, the national debt has doubled in four years of economic mismanagement by this government. She has the gall to

October 18, 1989
Government Orders
stand on her feet and suggest that this government's policy has been deficit reduction from day one.
Would the hon. member not agree with me that if that has been the policy that it has been a total and complete flop?

Madam Speaker, no, I will not agree with the hon. member that what the government has done is a total flop. I would assume that if you understand anything about finances, and being one of the members of the Liberal Party, you must realize the legacy you left to us. The interest that we pay each year on the debt, with the additional amount every year and compiling that amount, makes the debt that we have today an inheritance from your government.

speakerposition: Minister of Western Economic Diversification; Minister of State (Grains and Oilseeds)
speechtext:
Just a comment, Madam Speaker. The hon. member for Kingston and the Islands gets up and talks about what has gone on. Some of us were in this place when the hon. member's party was the government. We had interest rates of 22 per cent, 23 per cent, 25 per cent. We had an inflation rate at 11 per cent and 12 per cent.
If the member wants to talk about seniors, one of the most pernicious things that any senior citizen has to deal with is inflation. If we are talking about managing the economy, surely to goodness in terms of dealing with the seniors, which is one of the things he talked about, one of the things that we can do for seniors is to provide a stable economic environment so that when they get into their retirement years, some of that stability is there in the form of stable interest rates and reasonable inflation rates.

Madam Speaker, I must admit I am fascinated by the hon. minister's argument that it is okay to poke a person in the right eye now, because someone used to poke him in the left eye.
I must thank the hon. member for her vigorous and stimulating defence of the government's policy in this regard.
I must confess, however, that when listening I was reminded of the words of Humpty Dumpty in Lewis Carroll's Alice in Wonderland who said at one point-I believe I can recall this-"When I use a word, it means
precisely what I intend it to mean, neither more nor less". I was reminded of this in the member's use of the term "universality".
I would like to ask the member if her understanding of universality is the same as mine, which is to say that a universal program is a program that is available, without any hindrance, to all Canadians. Or in her use of the term, does it mean that it is in some way means-tested, as will be the case with the old age security program and the family allowance program, given the passage of this bill?

Madam Speaker, I think I have already answered that question. I stated earlier that all eligible seniors will receive the old age pension. Old age security is not something that will be determined to any one person by the amount of money he or she has at this time. Seniors will receive a cheque every month. The old age security cheque will not be discontinued because someone has an excess amount of money. People will receive those cheques.
The income tax department will look at the amount of money that a person has. If he or she can be taxed on an amount over $50,000, then, on a percentage basis, some of that money will be returned to the government.
I must also answer to the questioner, that when talking to the seniors in my riding, they are in agreement that the future generation and young people now need some of that money and they are very glad to share it with them.

Madam Speaker, it is a pleasure to rise and speak on this particular bill and to talk about the ramifications of this legislation. As one looks through and sees the size of this bill, one realizes right away that it is a far-reaching bill which deals with all sorts of things: income tax, federal-provincial fiscal arrangements, post-secondary education, old age security, and so on.
I think it reaches furthest into the pocketbooks of Canadians. It reaches furthest into the pocketbooks of the elderly and the young, the unemployed, the sick, and the students of this country. I feel badly about it too. I really do. I think it is a shock and a shame that this government would foist this type of legislation upon Canadians.
October 18, 1989

The clawback in particular is a breach of the Prime Minister's so-called sacred trust, a thing that would never happen. But the clawback is happening and is being implemented in this legislation. It is a shame because it is a direct attack on the elderly of Canada. They are the people who paid their way and supported this country and this government, and now they are repaid with a clawback.
The principle of universality has been destroyed by this legislation. It is shocking to say the least. If I can quote the Canadian Council on Social Development which said, back in April of this year, that by taking back the entire family allowance from 368,000 families and all of the old age security from 54,000 seniors and reducing these benefits for many more, the government is eroding the fundamental principle of universality which recognizes our collective responsibility for caring for children and for the elderly.
That is a shocking indictment of this government and what it has done. The clawback of family allowance will take up $1.68 billion from family budgets over the next five years, roughly $500 million a year by the year 1991. Those are families, in most cases, which cannot afford this loss and this reduction. Of course, the government will tell us that it will give it back, that it will have all of these fancy programs and ways to restore some of the money, but I say to you that it should not be taken in the first place. It should not have to be put back.
Some things are sacred. Some things ought not to be touched. Obviously we have to maintain that principle of universality. The party that I have the pleasure of working with and the riding that I have the pleasure of representing firmly believes that we should maintain the principle of universality.
I am also concerned about the effects of this legislation on higher education. Again, the Canadian Association of University Teachers said:
Higher education is, in fact, an investment as much as an expenditure. The Finance Minister talked in his budget about the effect on future generations. The effect of failing to compete with the Americans, the Japanese and many European countries in educational investment will be to ensure a future for our youth as hamburger flippers rather than as meaningful participants in the technological era that is upon us.
What is the effect of this legislation and the effect of stopping the movement of funds to higher education to the universities in our community? I happen to have one and my hon. friend from Beausejour has another. I can tell you from talking to the presidents of those universities that they have had to cut back on programs and cut
Government Orders
back on some of the education that their students are receiving. It is in large measure because this government is not fulfilling its obligation to higher education.
I also want to talk about the UI cuts in Bill C-21, and the effects of those cuts which are covered here in this legislation. Moncton was lucky, quite frankly, and had the legislative committee in that riding. We heard from a number of people who had concerns, but the impression that one is left with is that the committee wasted its time, that nothing really had any impact on what the government intended to do.
There is no guarantee that the UI program which has set up a training budget will see training done in New Brunswick. There is no guarantee that there will be any jobs once people are retrained. The government is taking money out of the pockets of New Brunswickers, and the unemployed who have contributed their funds to the unemployment insurance fund will end up in Ontario in Quebec and out west where the high-tech industries are looking for retraining in doing jobs. The effect of this legislation is to take money out of Atlantic Canada, out of New Brunswick, and put it where it is really not needed for retraining people, where there is an abundance of jobs and work.
It is a resettlement program.

It will force the people of Atlantic Canada and New Brunswick to move and to live in such places as Toronto, heaven forbid. This government hammers away at the people of Atlantic Canada. I think it is absolutely essential that there be an amendment to this legislation which would see the money that is taken from the workers of New Brunswick stays in New Brunswick for retraining and that there is new job creation and new opportunities for which these people can be retrained.
It was interesting that cabinet ministers from the New Brunswick government were not allowed to speak or to give their views at the hearings because somebody suggested that they may be grandstanding. The Hon. Russ King, Minister of Advanced Education in New Brunswick, spoke of the problem of illiteracy in New Brunswick and that because of the changes in the UI, people would have to give it up if they wanted to get training to improve themselves. They are in a Catch-22 situation because if they are illiterate, want to improve themselves and try to do something in a particular area it is going to cost them their UI. That will cost them the

October 18, 1989
Government Orders
opportunity to be retrained, which is the focus of this legislation.
