Needless to say, the changes in qualification times have very serious adverse effects on an area like New Brunswick. I know from discussions with my colleague from Beausejour that the seasonal workers in his riding, as well as in my own, are being very adversely affected by the UI changes.
What we have to look at in all of this is the ripple effect that this type of legislation has, with all the changes that have been put upon the people in the regions. There is less money for seniors. There is downgrading of education and health facilities in Atlantic Canada; changes to UI in effect hitting the people who can least afford it; losses of VIA Rail jobs and losses of VIA Rail passenger service in Atlantic Canada.
In my own riding the closure of the CNR shops is putting 1,200 people out of work. Now we have the allusion from a recent transport committee meeting that perhaps the Atlantic region is going to be closed and another 2,500 jobs will be lost to the Moncton riding. All of these things spill over the whole economy and have an adverse affect on the citizens of that economy.
This is bad legislation. It is hardship legislation. It is legislation that is going to be felt by Atlantic Canadians for a long time.
I think it is particularly interesting to look at the social benefits that this type of legislation is adversely affecting, particularly with the clawback. We look at the Prime Minister's campaign promise, and appropriately it was in Summerside, P.E.I. where they are really thrilled about the promises from the Prime Minister. Ele said: "As long as I am Prime Minister of Canada social benefits, especially those for the elderly, will be improved not diminished by our government."
What a commitment, and here is the proof of the commitment. You can see that the commitment was nothing but hollow and really negative as far as a
commitment to seniors in Atlantic Canada and in my riding is concerned.
In conclusion, the clawback is adverse, and the whole approach of this government as far as privatization is concerned, closing the bases, closing VIA Rail passenger service, all points to one thing. This government suffers from a rare disease called "deficititis". It is fighting the deficit on the backs of those who can least afford it, our seniors, the people who depend on a national rail service, the people in communities with military bases, and the people particularly in the regions who depend on a national, equitable UI system. This bill should be withdrawn.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as this debate on Bill C-28 continues and we hear from members of the opposition, I always feel the compulsion to rise in the House of Commons to put the facts on record in case anybody is actually listening to the ramblings of the hon. members opposite, particularly with respect to the change in the old age assistance taxation. They speak of the elderly, those who are in dire straits and need help, but what they never mention is the exact method of taxation, the fact that only those who receive old age assistance and whose incomes exceed $77,000 a year will be asked to pay back that part of the old age assistance which is not already taxed. In the case of an individual making over $77,000, I think it probably amounts to $1,500 or less which he or she is being asked to contribute.
Apparently, the hon. members want those people to keep that money, possibly at the expense of other Canadians who are really in dire need and need maintenance programs, special help and assistance, which this government is providing. They say in defence of their position, that we are breaching the golden rule of universality. I have said here, and I will say it again: you cannot eat universality, you cannot wear it, you cannot put it in the bank, you cannot improve your lifestyle with the concept of universality. Many think it is a sacred cow rather than a sacred trust.
The government has taken those steps to insure that Canada remains solvent, to insure that Canada, as a nation, is able to provide benefits to those in need. Yes, at the expense of those not in need. Yes, at the expense of people with incomes of $77,000 and more.
October 18, 1989

Does the hon. member disagree with the policy that takes money from people with incomes of $77,000 and gives it to those with no income or little income, who are really in need? Is he against that policy?
Hear, hear!

Madam Speaker, in a nutshell I disagree with any program and any piece of legislation that has the effect of taking money out of Atlantic Canada and putting it someplace where it is not needed. That is what my hon. friend is suggesting that we should do.
Sure he suggests that we should cut VIA so there are no passenger rail services in Atlantic Canada. He suggests that we should take all of the training money like UI and send it to Toronto-to Ontario-and to Montreal where it is not needed. That is what I am opposed to, and I will continue to fight that type of legislation. I am surprised that my hon. friend could support such terrible legislation for Atlantic Canadians.

Madam Speaker, the member opposite says that rich Canadians should not receive government benefits, that universality should not be directed toward rich Canadians. Well, his Prime Minister is a rich Canadian. In fact, he earns over $100,000 a year perhaps $140,000 a year. He is at the public trough. He has four children.
I would like to ask the hon. member, through my colleague, whether he believes that the Prime Minister of Canada is paying back, for example, the family allowance that he is receiving for his four children? He is a wealthy Canadian.
The bottom line is that senior citizens have a legal right to the old age security, and this government does not have the legal right or the moral right to take back what these people are entitled to, especially when the Prime Minister across the way is whistling and blowing at the same time. If he really believes that rich Canadians should not be receiving government benefits, why doesn't he give back to the people of Canada the family allowance that he receives every month?

Madam Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to rise in this House today representing the views and concerns of the people of Haldimand-Norfolk and to discuss Bill C-28.
Government Orders
I had the pleasure last week of talking to some senior citizens about this bill. I know the bill deals with a lot of different issues, but I want to centre on that one issue. The bill makes 59 different amendments to the Income Tax Act, and I cannot deal with them all. So I want to relate to you some of the experiences I had talking with senior citizens about what they felt about the whole clawback.
This government calls this bill tax reform. But I say it is nothing but a sham. It is a disguised way of increasing taxes and it is a way of increasing taxes on senior citizens, on those who least can afford it.
We hear the gibberish across the way, by the Conservatives, who keep talking about budget deficits and cutting back on the budget deficit and bringing down taxes. That is what they said prior to the election. They said our taxes would go down. Unfortunately, what they did not say was that the Conservative government, since 1984, has increased taxes some 31 times. I do not think that most Canadians, especially the senior citizens I talked to this week, feel badly about paying their fair share. Unfortunately, what we are seeing is a government that consistently attacks the same people, those who are least able to attack back.
I want to first look at the budget and at Bill C-28. I want to talk about what the finance minister has been saying about budgets. The finance minister indicated that this cut-back will affect only seniors with an annual income of $50,000 or more. Today, it may be $50,000 but what about tomorrow, what about next year?
We have already seen examples of the government making commitments and then breaking its promises. It could be $40,000. It could be $30,000. There is no commitment yet by this government to say specifically that it will keep the clawback at $50,000.
The government says that this program will still have universality. What the government is not admitting is that along with the pension cheque or the family allowance cheque, it is also sending out tax invoices. It is also taxing these people back. Granted, these people will still receive benefits and it is universality in that sense, but the government is taking it back underhandedly in other ways. I think that is wrong. Senior citizens, quite frankly,

Government Orders
recognize that fact and are not prepared to put up with it. It is not universality.
Seniors can hardly believe that this is taking place because of what the Prime Minister has said in the past. He said: "As long as I am Prime Minister, social programs, especially those for the elderly, will be improved, not diminished". I had a hard time explaining what he meant by that on behalf of the Prime Minister when I spoke with seniors in my riding. They could not understand how a Prime Minister who made that promise could then bring in legislation like Bill C-28 which directly takes away their income.
What these cuts mean is that some people at 75 years of age will pay a higher tax on their income than a 35 year old person with the same income. That is not right. Seniors want to know why that is the case. Using the finance minister's own formula, a 45 year old couple who now earns $28,000 a year will have to pay tax on their old age pensions when they retire. The people recognize that.
A 55 year old Canadian who is today earning $25,000 will have his old age pension completely taxed back at the age of 80. In 20 years, over two million Canadian seniors will have to pay tax on their old age pensions.
The President of the National Senior Citizens and Pensioners Association, an organization of seniors groups which represents half a million Canadian seniors, stated recently that seniors have been betrayed and misled by this government. That same point of view was echoed by many seniors in my riding. The president said that he views this proposal as a serious breach of faith by our government and an insidious effort to undercut the social security programs that on numerous times have been stated a sacred trust.
The coalition of Quebec seniors said that the pension clawback is discriminatory on the basis of age, unfair and contrary to the Charter of Rights and that it creates a steeper tax rate for seniors than for others at similar levels. Seniors who, with great difficulty have succeeded over the years in saving for their retirement, are being penalized.
That same feeling was echoed by many seniors in my riding. This government seems to be saying that Canadians should not count on the sacred social contract, that the sacred contract is no longer there. Do not count on
having a family allowance, do not count on having a pension when one reaches retirement.
Many seniors in my riding kept asking, "Didn't we pay into this? Didn't we throughout our lives pay into this? Why do we now not have the ability to get it back?" They cannot understand. They keep hoping that there must be some legal technicality that can help them out of this situation. They said that they fairly, and with the understanding they would get something back, paid into this, but now they are not receiving anything back. They want to know from this government why. Quite frankly, I agree with them. I do not know why. I ask the government, why is it now that it is taking away the pensions of our seniors?
I feel it is important that everyone pay his fair share of taxes. However, it should not be just the large corporations, richer Canadians, who are able to sneak around the tax system. Seniors asked me this past week why it is that large corporations over the years, especially in the last five years, have been able to evade taxes and why it is that they are being singled out as the ones who have to pay.
This proposal means that a senior with an income of $70,000 per year will be taxed differently than someone younger. That is not fair. Seniors want an answer from this government as to why that is. To date in this debate, I do not think we have heard anything from this government.
In conclusion, I want to point out the views of the seniors in my riding to whom I spoke in Simcoe this past week, seniors who say that over the years, they have fought for Canada in different wars, they have paid their taxes fair and square. They decided that they would go into this program and in fact they paid into this program, and they want their money out of the program now. They call upon this government to take a few moments and explain to them why it is that they are now the ones who are being pressured to bring down this government's debt which it has doubled since 1984.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, again I feel compelled to respond by way of a comment on Bill C-28. As you know, Act of Canada, but opposition members seem to focus in on the clause which enacts the new Section 180.2 with respect to old age assistance. Again, for reasons I have
October 18, 1989

already explained, I think facts should be put on the record.
Let me start this time, for the benefit of hon. members, with this fact. There are three million recipients of old age assistance in Canada. Of those three million recipients, 2,633,000 or 87.8 per cent will pay no tax at all under this new provision. Another almost 200,000 more will pay no tax. When we come to tax, 32,000 recipients will have their old age assistance, the amount of money given to them by the Government of Canada from the national treasury taxed back under this provision. Those
32.000	people have incomes in excess of $100,000. The government is asking people with incomes in excess of $100,000, 32,000 of them, to pay back their old age assistance payments which came from the treasury of the Government of Canada and from the taxpayers of Canada.
That is not even all that bad because it is already taxed back in the normal course a great proportion of the amount they received as part of the normal taxation system. I say to the hon. member, I do not see what the problem is. Does the hon. member believe that those
32.000	people earning over $100,000 a year should keep that money at the expense of other Canadians who need help from the Government of Canada? Is that what he thinks?

Madam Speaker, that is a ridiculous argument. I challenge the member to go back to his own riding, speak to the senior citizens, and ask them what they feel. Ask them if they feel that it is fair that this government takes away a program that was a sacred trust, that this Prime Minister had told them was a sacred trust. I challenge him to go back to the senior citizens in his riding and ask them. Have you been there? Have you asked them? Have you seen them? Have you talked to them? Have you asked them how they feel?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext: You show me a $100,000 income earner and I will talk to him.

Madam Speaker, that is ridiculous. I spoke with the seniors in my riding. They want to hear why this government broke its promise. This government promised them that these programs would be sacred but instead took them away from them. They want to know
Government Orders
why this government continues to make promises that are broken.

Madam Speaker, I did listen to the entire speech made by my hon. colleague. Unless I missed it, I might put this question about this despicable move that the government is making to take money back from the old age pensioners. Is it the hon. member's understanding that this $60,000, $50,000 or $70,000 is going to remain static or is this amount going to be increased every year as the inflationary rate diminishes the real value of the dollar? What I am asking is if indeed this amount which is today set at $50,000 will be worth $42,000 or $30,000 in the years to come? I wonder if the hon. member could address that question.

Madam Speaker, I thank the hon. member for his question. He is absolutely right. I thank him for his insight. In fact, this government has made no commitment whatsoever to keep it the same. In fact, over the next few years, that figure, because of inflation, will drop and so you are absolutely right.
These people who will be earning $35,000 during the next few years will have it taxed back. Seniors recognize this. Seniors come to me and I am sure they come to the hon. member and ask why the government is not promising something. They do not believe its promises anyway but they say there must be something to this. If the government is not making a correction here, then we have something to worry about in the years to come.

Madam Speaker, it is not with a great deal of pleasure that I feel compelled to stand up and speak in this debate. The actions of the government deserve to be rejected by all Canadians as the changes in Bill C-28, in fact, damage one of the most important constituents we have in this country.
In beginning my own contribution to this debate, I was thinking about how the government finds itself in the position where all of a sudden it has to turn on senior citizens in order to increase its revenue base. The government in 1984 was full of promise, full of national debate, full of lots of vigour towards changing the Canadian way. How did it change the Canadian way?
First of all, the Conservatives turned to all their friends at high income levels and said, "We are going to give you a tax cut. We are going to reduce the amount of

Government Orders
money you have to pay in taxes. We are going to allow you capital gains tax free."
Then they went to the corporate world and said, "Don't worry, we are going to reduce your taxes." All of a sudden, a recently created deficit of about $100 billion suddenly blossomed until right now we face the awful spectre of a $350 billion accumulated deficit within the next two to three years.
They then realized that they had a choice. They could go back to their friends and companions and say, "We have made a mistake. We have to start taxing capital gains. We have to start taxing corporations like we do individual families. We have to go back to high income earners. We have to take money back from you." No, they are traumatized by going back to tax these people. Or else they could go back into their revenue base and somehow or another pull back on expenditures. Every minister sits around the table and says, "Not me, not me" except, of course, for the Minister of Transport. He is very easy that way. He will let you take away VIA Rail. All the other ministers are protecting their own bailiwicks.
So we have a government which is both bankrupt in money and in ideas. Its solution is to increase taxation on seniors. People on the other side of the House refuse to look at it in that simple way. They are increasing the rate of taxation among seniors in this country.
People again say, "Well, listen, why not tax the people who are making all this money?" First of all, you have to remember that the support one Liberal government after another built up for universal programs in this country was based on that very premise, that they were universal. It means you had access to these programs no matter what your income level. It means that the average middle-class family, making somewhere between $40,000 and $100,000 a year, with two people working, feels secure, whether we are talking about medicare or about looking forward to their pensions. They felt that they were going to be looked after. One of the ways of keeping a generous coalition going in a country such as Canada is by making sure that the middle class feels they have a stake in the system.
This government, in its own cruel and miserable way, is taking away the middle class. It is going to make the
middle class feel insecure. It is going to make the middle class feel as if it is not going to have a stake in the system.
When you do not have a stake in the system, what happens? You begin to pull away your own support. When you do not get a service from the government, why do you pay taxes? One of the great issues in local politics in this country is the issue of policing, and one of the most difficult things to do is to make sure the middle class feels well policed so that the police can then turn around and use resources in poor areas.
It is the same thing with pensions. Why should a person paying a lot of taxes who is not getting a benefit from the pension system support somebody with less income? The answer is that they will not do it. This government understands it the same way that Margaret Thatcher understood it in England. You pull away the middle class, you privatize it, you make it feel like it can look after itself and you dismiss the poor with the back of your hand. We are going through the same process right now.
This bill has to be fought and opposed because it poses a threat, not only to working poor in this country, but to the middle class. If we want to continue as a country with national programs, we need people who pay taxes. We all know as politicians that people are upset with the high tax rate. We have to give those people an opportunity to see and to understand that the system is working for them.
We in the Manitoba caucus, the hon. members for Winnipeg North, St. Boniface, Winnipeg South Centre and Winnipeg-St. James, had a one-day seminar on pension reform last June. We were surprised by the number of groups which stepped forward to outline the problems of the pension system in Canada. It is not only a question of the clawback but also several other problems that have to be reformed.
In my own constituency, and I do not have to tell members who have been in the House for a long time that the former member for Winnipeg North Centre built a reputation for fighting for the poor of our constituency. Through one speech after another, he made the pensioners in Canada realize that the Government of Canada had to make a commitment to them and had to live up to that commitment. Since then, people on Selkirk Avenue, Main Street, Portage Avenue and Pritchard Avenue in Winnipeg understand that the role of
October 18, 1989

the federal government is to protect their pensions and to enhance their lifestyle.
They are now joined in Winnipeg North Centre by a new group of elderly who are not aged 65 but are aged 55. They are middle class families who come in from the suburbs and who need protection and income support. The neighbourhoods in Winnipeg North Centre will be transformed by older people such as these making a commitment to one of the oldest and poorest constituencies in this country. It is one that needs to be regenerated. These people have to work together and they have to feel they have a stake in the system. When you take money away unnecessarily, people lose their reason for supporting the system.
People often make light of the fact that the degeneration of income or the lack of an income base is only affected with the first 3 per cent. One of the demographic changes we have in this country is the number of people who live well past 65. For example, in Winnipeg North Centre, the people who come into the senior citizens' residences are often aged 81. They begin their life as seniors at age 81. They live to their mid-eighties. Let us say they live to the age of 85. Stop and think about it; you have your old age pension for 20 years and for each one of those years the government does not protect 3 per cent of your income. What is the erosion in your buying power for 20 years at 3 per cent per year accumulative? You have to realize that you will take a huge reduction in your living standard.
The minister from Manitoba, the minister responsible for western diversification, stood up earlier to remind the House of high interest rates back in the early eighties and pointed his finger across the floor saying he cannot believe that those on this side of the House were even worried about inflation nowadays, given what we did to the country. I would like to remind that member that the reality of inflation is that it can break out upon us at any time. It is not limited to that government or this government. The people who understand this better than anyone else are the seniors. The ravages of inflation haunt them because their income level is unprotected and that lack of protection is furthered by the government's action. On that particular item, I join my caucus in strongly opposing the government.
Government Orders
On a second issue, the government has again failed in this legislation to address the question of fair taxation in the corporate world. While I do not join my friends in the NDP in ranting and raving against the corporate world, I do think there is a frustration in the middle management in Canada, people working in all-Canadian firms, who cannot see fair taxation in the corporate world. International corporations, because of the financing, marketing and the legal structures, are able to move capital and tax dollars out of Canada. Until this government is willing to bring into the House legislation which addresses this issue of lost income, lost taxation, we will continue to find ourselves in the comer, having insufficient money to help those Canadians who need help the most.
There are two major faults with this piece of legislation; its inability to protect seniors at all income levels and to understand their needs for income protection far into the future, and the refusal of the government to deal with corporations and the extraction of proper corporate taxation rates that will enhance the revenue base of the federal government.

Madam Speaker, this bill marks one of the most significant changes in social policy in Canada in the last several decades. In sum, it eliminates the universal nature of two important social programs.
In the few minutes that I have today, I would like to focus on several aspects. I would like to focus on the government's recent promises concerning social programs, what the clawback is and how it works, what the government claims about the clawback, how the clawback will attack not just the rich, but ordinary Canadians everywhere in a very short time, and some alternatives the government could have considered.
Let us begin by looking at the government's promises about social programs. Most Canadians remember the Prime Minister's sombre assurance that social programs were a "sacred trust". Others remember this government assuring Canadians that it would improve social programs in general and improve the lot of seniors in particular. Let me remind people of two of these solemn assurances.
One is reported by the Canadian Press on March 7, 1984, when the Prime Minister said:
Our position is simple and straightforward. We are in favour of
universality in social programs and it shall not be touched.

October 18, 1989
Government Orders
Again, on October 15, 1988, speaking to seniors in Summerside, Prince Edward Island, the Prime Minister said:
Let me say a special word to the senior citizens. In the future Canada will be doing more, not less, for all of you.
He said this. I am not making this up.
As long as I am Prime Minister of Canada, social benefits, especially those for the elderly, will be improved, not diminished by our government which is committed to social justice and fairness for Canadians.
Especially for the elderly, note.
So what about this bill? We are not talking small potatoes here, much as the government would like you to believe that we are. We are talking about a dramatic shift in the direction of this country. We are talking about ending the universality of social programs in Canada.
And we are talking especially about literally stealing the pension savings of older Canadians. I quote, because he stated it so much better than I could, from a letter by Mr. David Wilson of Winnipeg to that city's Winnipeg Free Press. He writes in part:
The old age security program was initiated in the early 1950s as a contributory program which paid for itself, with each year's payments funded by matching contributions. A special tax was created for this purpose, and each time the pension was raised the tax was raised as well. Up to 1972 this line was included on the income tax form: "Old age security-4 per cent of taxable income-maximum $240." It is also very likely that we continued to pay this tax after 1971, but it was not a separate item on the income tax forms.
The federal government has now ruled that the old age security pension can be taxed away from pensioners who have paid for it.
Not only is this a betrayal of what was previously deemed a sacred trust by this government, it is a theft from the very seniors who paid into the program for so many years.
We will get to the details of how the bill will work in a moment, but given that there is such a shift, such a substantial change in policy, would you not expect an honest government, a government that is straightforward with its people, to have a national discussion about this? Then, after, the pros and cons have been discussed, announce to the people of Canada what steps it plans to take? But no, this government's long suit is neither honesty nor openness. The announcement of this shift was made among an avalanche of bad news announcements in the budget, and there had been no substantial public consultation beforehand. Indeed, the Tory chairman of the finance committee admits this, even if the PM won't.
In a wonderfully candid moment, the chairman wrote to a resident of Edmonton. In his letter to Mr. William Daly, a 61-year old resident of Edmonton he said:
We have decided to eliminate universality and we do that in a sense by the clawback in both family allowance and the old age pension.
How admirably honest. Even if the government is not, obviously members of it are. He continues:
As you know, it has been a Conservative philosophy for some time that distributions from the state ought to go essentially to those in need. While the clawback may be unfair and sneaky, it is there.
An admirable honesty, wholly uncharacteristic of his benchmates.
As we had graphically demonstrated for us earlier this afternoon, the term "universality" is sometimes misunderstood. Perhaps it might be helpful to describe what is generally meant when we say a program is universal. Simply put, a universal program is one that delivers benefits to all Canadians, regardless of income. Why do this? Why not discriminate on the basis of income? The reasons change as one moves from program to program, but for the family allowance those reasons are principally two.
First, universality is the recognition by the Canadian people through their government of the contribution that parents at all income levels make to raising Canada's future citizens. Second, it also recognizes in some small way that extra expenses are incurred by parents for raising children that childless couples and single people do not have.
As for the universality of the old age security program, that recognizes the contribution that all elderly Canadians, whatever their financial circumstances, have made to our society.
Now, it is true that although these two programs currently deliver the same monthly cheque to all their recipients, family allowance and OAS do not now provide the same benefit to all beneficiaries. This is because the benefits from both those programs are counted as taxable income. As a result many families and pensioners pay federal and provincial income tax on those benefits and, consequently, benefits after taxes of these programs are highest for lower income beneficiaries and lowest for

higher income beneficiaries. Every recipient now gets some meaningful benefit.
In fact tax filers in the top income bracket still end up with a substantial 55 per cent of the benefits, a situation due mainly to the grotesque distortions introduced into the income tax system by successive Liberal and Conservative governments.
However, under the new scheme above a certain income level higher income families and pensioners will have to pay back 100 per cent-the entire shot-of the benefits they received over the course of the previous year. The government has taken great pains to suggest that this is no big deal, that it will not affect many people at all.
We have heard that in the questions and comments following the remarks of previous speakers. And, according to the Budget Papers, on page 9, the clawback of family allowance and old age security payments will have a minimal effect on individual Canadians and families.
The finance minister claims, for example, that only 4.3 per cent of seniors will be paying back any part or all of their pensions, with 54,000 individuals paying back all of their OAS and 74,000 paying back a part of it. On family allowances he claims that only 14 per cent of families will be affected, with 368,000 paying back all of their family allowance and 167,000 paying back a part of it. Thanks to normal inflation, these numbers in both cases will go up rapidly year by year so that more and more retirees will end up repaying their pensions and more and more families will repay all their family allowance.
The way the system works is that the income level at which the clawback starts will move upwards according to the same deindexing formula that exists in the tax system; in other words inflation minus 3 per cent and that is the key, Mr. Speaker. This means that if you assume an inflation rate of 4.5 per cent the income limit will move up by only 1.5 per cent in that year, 4.5 per cent minus 3 per cent. That is not indexing, and that means that inflation will erode the clawback floor.
Government Orders
A worker earning $40,000 a year and watching his or her income rise with inflation would be earning enough to put his or her income over the clawback level for family allowances by 1997. For retirees, the clawback is more complex and phases in more slowly, but a simple rule of thumb is that a worker earning $28,000, that is roughly the average industrial wage, will be hit by the clawback by the time he or she retires.
This assumes that income keeps pace with inflation and that retirement income is 70 per cent of pre-retirement income. Once again the government accomplished this by not fully indexing the trigger figure of $50,000. Over time, through inflation, more and more of us will be caught.
Here are some other examples. A 30 year old making $30,000 will have part of her OAS pension clawed back when she retires at 65. The same is true for 35 year olds making $35,000, 40 year olds making $40,000, and 45 year olds making $45,000 a year. All told the clawback will catch about 128,000 Canadian pensioners in 1990. In 20 years that will rise to over one million Canadian pensioners.
In regard to family allowance a similar pattern applies. Assume that you are presently 23 years old and that you are making just over $25,000 a year. If you have children in five years and you never make more than that income, adjusted for inflation you will be losing part of the family allowance payment by the time your child is 18.
In 1990 roughly 14 per cent of families will have their family allowance subjected to the clawback. In 10 years that will rise to nearly 30 per cent. The proportion of families affected by the clawback will more than double within 10 years.
These examples are based on very conservative estimates of income growth and, no doubt, understate the case, I should point out.
The point is that the clawback does not maintain the principle of universality as Mulroney and Wilson contend. It marks the steady erosion of our social programs down to a much lower common denominator. Henceforth all social programs will be for the poor only. They will be targeted to those in need or deemed to be in need and thereby made selective, not universal. The clawback will move our pension system closer to that of the U.S. There, workers are covered by contributory pensions like

October 18, 1989
Government Orders
our CPP or by means tested programs like our GSI, but not by a universal pension program like our OAS. No pension exists in the U.S. as a right of citizenship for those over 65.
This point is central: it has been Michael Wilson's mission as finance minister to shatter the universality barrier. Once that principle is gone, then it is a very simple matter to refine the clawback even further and make the program more and more selective by taxing back higher and higher levels of benefits.
The National Council on Welfare issued an excellent report in September 1989 entitled The 1989 Budget and Social Policy. It highlights some of the very damaging effects that this policy will have.
I have mentioned a few. I would like to refer to its report in a little more detail to outline a few more. First, the clawback will erode the principle of horizontal equity. One of the reasons for paying child benefits to all families including the better-off is to recognize their additional financial burden in raising children as compared with childless couples and single persons at the same level of income.
This is known as the principle of horizontal equity. After the clawback the only benefit available to all higher income parents will be the $66 per child non-refundable child tax credit. Clearly removing family allowances from better-off families will put them at a greater disadvantage vis-a-vis childless couples and singles who have the same income but no child rearing expenses.
Second, the clawback will discriminate against one-earner families. A one-earner family with an income of $56,000 and two children will have to return 100 per cent of its family allowance benefits to the federal government once the clawback is fully phased in, in 1991. However a two-earner couple with two children in which one spouse earns $45,000 and the other spouse $35,000, for a joint income of $80,000, will not have to pay the clawback because the higher income parents' net income is under the $50,000. Instead, the family will be subject only to the normal rate of taxation on its family allowances returning about 45 per cent of its benefits to the federal and provincial governments. The clawback is both unjust and illogical. The one-earner couple at $56,000 will pay back all of its family allowance. The
two-eamercouple earning $80,000, $24,000 more, gets to keep over half of its family allowance.
Third, the clawback will add to the complexity of the child benefits system. Over the past four years the Minister of Finance has further complicated an already complex child benefit system. In brief, the non-refundable child tax credit which replaced the children's tax exemption in 1988 is $66 for each of the first two children and $132 for the third and subsequent children. Families with incomes under $16,000 now receive their refundable child tax credit in two instalments while other families continue to get it only once a year. Children under age seven qualify for a $200 supplement to the refundable child tax credit in 1989 so there are now two rates. It is $565 for children over seven and $765 for those under seven. Parents with receipted child care expenses can claim a maximum $4,000 child deduction for each child under seven, but only up to $2,000 for children aged seven through fourteen.
Last, family allowances and both the refundable and non-refundable child tax credits are now indexed only by the amount of inflation over 3 per cent a year. Confused? The Lord knows I am, and I assume many of the parents of this country are.
Fourth, before the clawback there were two types of families receiving family allowances. Families too poor to owe income tax kept all of their family allowances while those which pay tax kept part of their family allowances and returned the rest to federal and provincial governments in the form of income taxes paid on their benefits.
After the clawback there will be four types of families receiving the family allowance. There will be families which keep all their family allowances because they are too poor to owe income tax. There will be those which keep part of their family allowance because they pay regular income taxes on their benefits. There will be those who keep part of their family allowance because they pay both regular income taxes and the clawback on their benefits. There will be those which will have to pay back all of their family allowances through the clawback.
This is part of what we have had heralded for us as a simpler and more easily understood tax system. This attack on universality is at very least ill-conceived, but it is more than that, and it is worse than that. There are a number of very important questions which need to be raised about this issue. For example, why should an individual be entitled to receive $100,000 in capital gains tax-free but lose the $4,000 he or she gets in OAS simply

because it was paid as a universal social benefit? Family allowances and old age security are already taxed in Canada. Why should a special tax be levied on children and on the elderly?
What will "the unique identity of Canada" mean in a few years when our social programs exist only to serve those in need? Will not our social programs be just like those in the U.S., leaner and meaner as all means tested programs are? How long will the population support the maintenance of social programs from which they are effectively excluded as beneficiaries? Will "need" be redefined downwards as it has been in Britain and in the U.S. and as it has been already with our UI and our welfare programs provincially?
If the essence of universality is destroyed through the back door, what is to protect medicare from attack? Will Canada's sick have to prove they are also "in need" to have access to our health care system? When did Canadians vote for having means tested family allowance and old age security programs? When was that put to them in any honesty at all?
Again, remember what the Prime Minister has said, defending the attempted deindexation of pensions in 1985. In Hansard, at page 5774 for that year, he said:
There is not a single elderly person in this country today who has been impacted unfavourably by this budget.
We will pass over that. Referring to the member asking the question, he said:
I have given him full responses to assure him that the commitment of this government to the elderly and the integrity of social programs is unrivalled and unsurpassed by any other party in the House and certainly is no less than anyone else's.
Or, how about the hon. member who chairs the finance committee, who said: "They", which is to say seniors, "live at a slower pace and they don't spend money in the same sense that you and I do. Older people don't wear out their clothes. They have plenty of money but they don't like to spend it".
Government Orders
Mr. Blenkam apparently has forgotten that 42.7 per cent of single pensioners live below the poverty line in Canada, but we will let that pass as well.
I think actually in that statement from Mr. Blenkam, which I quoted earlier, he got it right. This government is, in his words, sneaky. It simply cannot be trusted to do what it says it is going to do.
I know the Prime Minister tries valiantly to paint the picture that he really cares about seniors and families in Canada, and his government has no alternative but to eliminate universality in social programs. That is the cry, the justification: "The deficit made us do it". What utter bunk. The alternatives are staring us in the face.
Just imagine raising additional money by attacking social programs, asking someone with a $100,000 income to forgo $270 per child in current family allowances, instead of introducing a fourth marginal tax rate of 32 per cent for high income earners, which would raise some $2,000 each or $300 million a year.
Imagine setting up a system that will lead Canadians to fight against Canadians instead of reducing the interest rate by 2 per cent, which would raise an additional $3.5 billion a year.
In conclusion, I entered this debate principally to voice the feelings of disgust and rage that I know characterize seniors in my riding and that I feel safe in assuming characterize seniors across this country. They know that this clawback provision, this bill in its entirety, is unjust. They are telling that to the government. The only question before the House is whether or not the government will have the guts to listen.

Madam Speaker, with a great deal of trepidation I will ask the member a question. Going through the legislation I noticed the changes in the rules dealing with the surtax. This was brought to my attention by several constituents who were concerned that the government had very quietly changed its opinion as to what to do with the surtax. The temporary 3 per cent surtax on personal income taxes was imposed in 1986. In the 1987 budget the Minister of Finance promised that when the new sales tax was introduced the personal and corporate income taxes would be removed. That is a quotation from the Minister of Finance in the House of Commons on June 18, 1987.

October 18, 1989
Government Orders
Now the minister has made the personal income surtaxes a permanent feature of the income tax system. Before the GST technical paper was released the Minister of Finance had promised to remove the surtax as part of the GST package, but that promise has been broken and the surtaxes are now a permanent tax on all Canadians.
The increase in the surtax from 3 per cent to 5 per cent will take another $1.1 billion out of Canadians' incomes, or an average of more than $100 per Canadian family. The surtaxes, in my opinion, defeat the minister's own stated objectives of tax reform. One of the government's objectives of stage one of tax reform was to lower personal income tax rates. The top marginal tax rate was lowered from 34 per cent to 29 per cent. However the imposition of the surtaxes on all Canadians has pushed the marginal tax rates back up to close to what they were before tax reform started.
The minister sold tax reform to Canadians by telling them that they would get lower personal income tax rates but would pay more sales tax. Canadians have the sales tax increases all right but not any of the savings as promised. I would just like to ask my friend what he thinks about the government reneging on its original promise to drop the surtax as it introduced the GST.

Madam Speaker, I would like to say that it took me completely by surprise, but I realize that in this House we are honourable and must tell the truth so I cannot say that.
If I were to take every broken promise uttered by this government and record it in Hansard, I would have enough Hansard to wallpaper my home back in Edmonton. So, is it a surprise? No. Is it characteristic of this government? Yes. Do I expect it to be the last broken promise? No. Do I expect that in breaking these promises the government is going to change its spots and in fact start benefiting ordinary Canadians? No. Do I expect that it will continue its assumed mandate of altering the taxation system to make it ever more unfair, ever more oppressive of ordinary middle and low income Canadians in the interests of high income Canadians? Yes. And, by the way, I would be really cautious about defending high income Canadians if I were the hon. member, because they have more than enough defenders across the way.
They suffer an embarrassment of riches in this regard too. I think I will let it go there.

Madam Speaker, I want to make a couple of comments and ask for a couple of remarks from the veiy eloquent member who just spoke, who I am honoured to say is a colleague of mine.
Two or three years ago in the last Parliament we debated the cut-backs and erosion of social programs, particularly the family allowance and the old age pension, when the government at that time was deindexing. I was struck at the time by the fact that the senior citizens across the country organized and were able to change policy. However children have no vote and they really have no voice so it is much more difficult to organize.
The deindexation of the old age pension was stopped. The deindexation of the family allowance went forward. I am glad to hear the hon. member speak so eloquently on behalf of children in the country. I would remind him that when the family allowance was first brought in by the members of this party, largely, and by social democrats and others across the country, the intent was that it would grow and would gradually become a way of subsidizing the real cost of child rearing in this country. It was based on the philosophy that children belong to all of us.
I do not happen to have children, but I feel I have just as much responsibility, if not more, to pay taxes for the cost of rearing Canada's children. It is very, very unfair, therefore, to hit the parents who have the high costs of raising children with the high cost of housing, clothing, education, and so on, regardless of their income. It is very unfair to be taking this back only from them and not taking it out of general tax revenues.
Another point that has come into this debate in the past is the fact that the family allowance usually goes to mothers. It is often the only cheque that the woman, even of well-to-do families, receives in her own name. We heard some very eloquent statements from women on that aspect.
A further point that I think has come into the argument from time to time, and he perhaps touched on it, is that this is really doing away with universality. I would go further and say that it is doing away with a floor of social security in this country altogether. As social policy analysts have said, "if you do not have the middle class involved in some of the benefits from social
October 18, 1989

programs, you lose political support and pretty soon the programs are coming down with tougher means tests and there is a great stigma on the kind of programs that go to people; we would be back to a dog eat dog society".
Perhaps my hon. colleague would care to comment.
Me too, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak on behalf of the senior citizens in my riding and on behalf of families and their children.
I will now address to Bill C-28, an act to amend the Income Tax Act.

Bill C-28 makes 59 different amendments to the Income Tax Act, implementing many of the 1989 budget provisions.

Madam Speaker, to me, these changes in the Income Tax Act are an attack on universality, on senior citizens and on our families.
As of financial year 1990-91, the government will effectively put an end to the universality of social benefits in Canada. People who paid a special tax before 1971 to help pay for old age security benefits received the assurance of Parliament, when the tax reform was passed in 1971, that they would continue to be entitled to old age security benefits.
Last year, during the election campaign, the Prime Minister said repeatedly that he would not tamper with old age security pensions. He also said: "As long as I am Prime Minister of Canada, social benefits, especially those for the elderly, will be improved, not diminished by our government". That is the promise the Prime Minister made, the promise the whole country heard during the televised debate. At one point he even brought along his mother, repeating his promise that he would protect old age security pensions and would never tamper with them.
Incredibly, since the 1988 election the Tories have yet to keep a single promise they made to Canadians. They never mentioned this during the campaign. Never! They
Government Orders
were playing a very different tune, which is why I say we cannot trust them.
Bill C-28 is an attack on the rights of senior citizens. It is an attack on the pensions they deserve. This Bill is an attack on family allowances and on our families.
This Bill is an attack on the principle of universality of the social programs we designed and implemented many years ago.
Madam Speaker, this bill is a complete denial of the promises the Prime Minister made during the last election campaign, as I said earlier. I would like to recall, for the benefit of hon. members, the promise the Prime Minister made in Sydney, Nova Scotia, during the last election campaign. He said: "As long as I am Prime Minister, social benefits, especially those for the elderly, will be improved, not diminished".
Bill C-28 is a betrayal of what the Prime Minister once called a sacred trust.
This is what my Liberal party leader had to say during the election campaign: "The men and women of Canada who worked all their lives to build this country counted on the old age security pension as one of their rights as Canadian citizens. They paid taxes all their lives. They planned their future on the basis of this pension. It is part of the social contract in Canada."

Bill C-28 makes 59 different amendments. Part 1.2 of clause 48 of this bill implements the clawback of family allowances and old age security pensions. The amount of the repayment is equal to 15 per cent of the taxpayer's net income over $50,000. The clawback of the family allowance will take $1,686 billion out of family budgets in the next five years, or $500 million a year by 1991.
Within 10 years close to one million Canadian families who currently receive family allowances or old age pensions will begin to lose their benefits due to the partial indexing of the $50,000 threshold.
The $50,000 threshold at which individuals begin paying their family allowance and old age security benefits is only partially indexed. This deindexation of the $50,000 threshold means that within 10 years close to one million Canadians will start losing their family allowances and the old age pensions. The clawback proposal would put a special tax on families with children

Government Orders
and on seniors, a tax that does not apply to anyone else. In this way the clawback is anti-family and anti-senior.
The National Council on Welfare in a press release dated September 13, 1989 stated:
The federal government should abandon its proposed "clawback" of family allowances and Old Age Security pensions.
The move away from universal benefits is the most significant change in social policy in a generation, yet it was announced by the Minister of Finance in the budget speech with no prior consultation.
In the case of seniors, the federal government had publicly rejected the idea of a clawback or surtax on old age pensions as late as January 1985 on the grounds that it would "seriously disrupt" the retirement income system-the clawback changes the rules of the game without their consent. The elderly have already paid for their old age pensions through a lifetime of paying income taxes.
In the case of parents, the clawback discriminates against one earner families because it is based on individual net income. A one earner family with two children and a net income of $56,000 would lose all its family allowance benefits. A two earner couple where one spouse earns $45,000 and the other $35,000 would escape the clawback despite their combined income of $80,000.
Second, I would like to read from a letter dated June 23,1989, which was sent to the Prime Minister from from Les Batterson, president of the Senior Citizens Federation. It stated:
Our position is that the tax-back is age biased, grossly inequitable and has serious implications with regard to universality.
We view this proposal as a serious breach of faith by our government and an insidious effort to undercut the social security programs that you have on numerous times stated are a sacred trust.
We also are aware that we had previous deficits as serious as the present one and the government of the day did not tax back pensions to which Canadians had every reason to believe they had a genuine right.
The Coalition of Quebec Seniors in a letter to the Minister of Finance dated May 24, 1989 stated:
As the clawback begins to affect increasing numbers of individuals, there can be no doubt that the net effect will be a gradual reduction of the principle of universality.
We consider further that a special tax which is only directed at seniors is discrimination on the basis of age, unfair, and contrary to the Charter of Rights.
Your proposal creates a steeper tax rate for seniors than for others at similar income levels. Seniors who with great difficulty have succeeded over the years in saving for their retirement are being penalized.
Madam Speaker, thank you for giving me this opportunity to speak on behalf of the senior citizens, the families and the young people in my riding.

Madam Speaker, I would like to thank my colleague for his very eloquent speech on the harm this bill will do to seniors in our country. He also reminded the government of principles which it seems to have forgotten: universality, equity and keeping prior commitments.

I would like to respond to a comment which was made repeatedly by my colleague opposite, the member for Halifax West. The argument that we hear repeatedly advanced on the other side of the House about the clawback measure, in particular, and the tax back on the family allowance, is that it is designed to tax the rich in order to give more money to the poor. I would like to ask, where is the money going to the poor? Everybody is being taxed more. The goods and services tax will be regressive. It will tax the poor citizens of this country, especially those in Atlantic Canada, proportionately more than it will tax the rich.
A whole litany of consumption taxes are being raised which we know will affect those with modest means much more than those with higher incomes. This line that we hear from the government is simply sophistry and designed to confuse what is really a tax grab from those people who are unable to avoid the tax.
The people who do not get taxed in this society are those who have the money to pay for tax lawyers, accountants, or who are members of large corporations that can avoid the tax. Let us face it, the government is unwilling to put in measures to obtain tax revenue from those who have it because it is much easier to tax those who, for various reasons, cannot avoid the tax.

The idea that this tax on old age security is a way of somehow making the system more fair is nonsense. Perhaps my colleague would like to comment on that in the time that remains.

Madam Speaker, I appreciate the comments of my colleague from Cape Breton Highlands-Canso. I think that we are talking about basic principles. And if the principle of universal social programs was established some time ago, we must stick to it, because a few years ago, senior citizens were much younger. They were then careful to put money aside, to invest well and all of a sudden, when they are retired and unable to react financially or politically or in any other way towards the government, they are hit in the pocket-book.
I think that if we want to raise taxes, if we must raise taxes, it is all right to raise taxes, then this must be done according to people's income and not because they get money from some source or another or in one way or another.
People must be taxed on their total income and not a particular aspect of it, like the amounts given under our social contract, family allowances or old age pensions. That is contrary to the principle of universality, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, I rise to discuss the bill proposed by the government. When I was glancing through the government report, one thing came to mind. It has been the argument of the government that one of the main reasons why it has to cut programs and projects that cater to people who are in need is because of the deficit.
Over the weekend, I was glancing at some documentation published by Statistics Canada, and also some documents published by different well-respected agencies.
In my view, to reduce the deficit, you just do not launch an assault on those who are keeping the economy rolling. Unfortunately, over the past five years the government has been panicking, and as a result it has been reactionary. It has launched an assault on middle income Canadians who are, to a large extent, the engine of the economy in this country.
Government Orders
Over the past 20 years we have seen a drastic decline in the manufacturing sector and a drastic increase in the service sector. I might add that this is the source of the problem in Canada and that is why the government is in a panic situation. If we were to increase the level of productivity, we would not be in this situation.
In the 1970s the manufacturing sector in Canada employed approximately 31 per cent of the workforce. In 1989-1990, it employs approximately 25 per cent of the workforce. This will decline to approximately 20 per cent of the workforce by the year 2000.
In the 1970s the service sector employed about 36 per cent of the labour force; by the year 2000, it will employ approximately 53 per cent. So there is a massive shift of the labour force from the industrial sector to the financial sector or the service sector.
This has caused a panic. Why? Because in the service sector more emphasis has to be put on education, and a more educated workforce is required to carry on with the tasks. According to a Globe and Mail report published on September 5, 1989, we cannot take pride in the fact that we are doing enough in the area of education in order to tackle the deficit.
The report states that more than 22 per cent of Canadians over the age of 15 are not currently enrolled in any kind of educational system or they are considered to be functionally illiterate. Furthermore, approximately 30 per cent of Canadian students who enter secondary education leave without getting a diploma. In comparison, Germany has about 14 per cent. Only 72 per cent of Canadians at age 17 are still enrolled in some form of formal education, compared to 94 per cent in Japan. If we want to compare ourselves to our friends in the south, the worker in the United States has at least one year more of education than the Canadian worker.
The shocking thing is that per capita Japan has four times as many engineers as Canada, but we have 20 times as many lawyers as Japan. Probably that is the problem, we have too many lawyers not have enough engineers.
It was quite disappointing to see a decline in the area of investment for education. Last year there was approximately an 1.8 per cent increase in the area of education, and when we compare that to the years between 1985 and 1989, we only had an increase of about 2.3 per cent,

October 18, 1989
Government Orders
which was well below the consumer price index of 4.2 per cent. Frankly, that is where the problem is.
We do not have an agenda for the future. We seem to be panicking. We seem to be pushing all the buttons at the same time when we do have the answer. We are all talking about the answer. The Prime Minister has been speaking for the past goodness knows how many years about the need for a better educational system, the need for standards, the need for more research and development, and the need for industry and private sector involvement. We are all saying a lot, but the government is not doing anything about it. That is what needs to be done. By investing more in the area of educational research and development, I can assure you that the train will start moving.
What we are doing is putting on all the brakes at the same time. We are increasing taxes. We do not have any other source of revenue except taxes as it is right now, and as a result we are going into the pockets of those who cannot help themselves. Unfortunately, in this particular case, it is our seniors, it is the middle-income earners.
I will challenge the minister in three years to tell me that one of the main reasons why they introduced the goods and services tax is to reduce the deficit. He should say that and he should tell Canadians that that is the main reason why it was introduced.
Who are the people who will be affected the most by this? It is the middle and low-income Canadians. It is quite unfortunate that the government has to claw back from those people who have built this country, who put in the infrastructure of this country. We have worked extremely hard in the Liberal party in the past 50, 60 and 70 years to build a middle-income group and to help those who need it. We introduced the social programs with the support of some of our colleagues in this House. We have them in place. Over the past four years, we have seen an assault that this country has never seen in its history.
This is a very, very sad thing to do. I have been to approximately 30 different town hall meetings in my riding with senior citizen groups. These people have attacked the government for its initiative to tax them and to take away their money. After all, it is the senior citizens' money.
Nobody could have put it better than a senior citizen in an article published in Today's Seniors of September 19, 1989. He said: "Having diligently saved for my retirement, it is most discouraging to find that instead of the enjoyment of the life I have saved for I will be contributing to bail out this spendthrift government." That is true.
Another senior said: "For the first time in my life I am frightened of the future." We are frightened of the future. Unless this government sets a proper agenda for the people of Canada, unless the government communicates the proper vision for Canada, unless the government stops looking at other means and ways than taxation then we are frightened of the future. I want to give the chance to some of my colleagues to address this particular bill, but I am frightened by what I see. I hope my colleagues from across the floor will also speak out on this issue.
Our senior citizens are hopeless. They need the support of all of us.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to rise in my place and participate in the debate on Bill C-28.1 want to add my voice to those of my colleagues in this House who have, in as profound a way as they could, drawn the attention of the House to the enormous betrayal that is represented by the piece of legislation put before Parliament, the quite profound disillusionment that Canadians feel at seeing the 59 amendments contained within this bill.
Bill C-28 is not a bill that deals merely in dollars and cents, although ultimately that is the impact, one of dollars and cents. It is not a bill that is primarily financial in nature, although Canadians will count and be able to count in quite dramatic ways the dollars and cents lifted out of their pockets, the decrease in their spending power, but the bill is ultimately not about money. This bill is ultimately about what kind of Canada we are going to live in during the 1990s and beyond. That is really what the bill is about.
We see increasingly in this country quite strong signs of renewed intolerance, renewed lack of understanding, lack of sensitivity. We are seeing a different kind of Canada emerge through the latter part of the 1980s, and it is interesting, through the five or six years that this Conservative administration has been the Government of Canada. In the House of Commons we frequently see members stand up with tens of thousands of names on petitions protesting the fact that a distinguished, honourable and decent human being who wants to be an RCMP officer cannot because religious requirements are such that he must wear a turban. That says something rather disheartening about what this country is coming to. We
October 18, 1989

see a chairman of a standing committee of this House describe the contributions of Canadians from a particular region to the work of that committee as not worth hearing. That says something rather disquieting about this House and this country.
There was a time not so long ago when those kinds of petitions-referring to turbans-or those kinds of comments from a distinguished parliamentarian just would not have been heard. But we are living in a different kind of country. Tolerance is disappearing.
Wrapped up in the 59 amendments to Bill C-28, wrapped up in the whole notion of clawback, wrapped up in the whole effort to pick the pockets of those least able to defend themselves, children and our senior citizens, is an example set by the government of that intolerance, that lack of caring, that insensitivity, that evolution of a new kind of Canada.
What kind of Canada is it? It is a Canada exemplified by those examples I cited, a Canada where citizens are taught to say I am okay, Jack, and that is all that matters. I can cut it. I have a roof over my head. I have bread and butter on the table and I am okay and it really doesn't matter a damn how my neighbour is. The same kind of mentality says you can define or defend culture on the basis of whether or not an RCMP officer, duly trained, properly equipped, is less an officer because he wears a turban for religious purposes. Intolerance!
That is what Bill C-28 is, a mean-spirited bill. It is intolerable. It says that the concept of universality does not matter any more. It. says that the Prime Minister's commitment to a sharing, caring, tolerant Canada doesn't matter any more. It says that the collection of values that have bound us together through all of these decades even within our diversity do not matter any more. It says that we are a different kind of country.
Canadians who are concerned about the clawback, Canadians who oppose clawing back those pension benefits from senior citizens acquired over a lifetime, do not oppose it just because we feel that a contract is a contract. That happens to be one good argument that somebody who paid all his life in the expectation of receiving "x" number of dollars ought to receive it because a contract was made and ought not to be broken.
Government Orders
That is not the only reason you defend somebody who has a high income in his or her senior years and say that pension ought not to be taken away.
We do not defend the family allowance moneys being clawed back thereby taking from children, because, we say, even though somebody has a reasonably good family income he or she ought to get paid every cent. We all know the family allowances are already taxed back now up to 30 per cent under the income tax system. That is not the reason we are defending, as the government would have us believe, the well-to-do in this society.
The reason we oppose the clawback, the reason we want social programs to remain universal, is that we know in this party and we have historically known in this country-indeed the Conservative Party across the way used to know or at least pretended to know-that a social program targeted only to the poorest of those among us is going to be a damn poor program. That is the reason we stand and oppose this bill. Because all senior citizens in Canada who have followed this debate know, including the poorest of Canada's seniors, that if you claw back the benefits of Canada's upper-income senior citizens and you claw back out of homes the family allowances of Canada's upper or middle-income people then you have clawed away a large part of the notion of sharing and caring in this country and you are ghettoizing through our social programs those people who are the poorest among us. You are saying that you are designing a program that will only apply to the poor. That is exactly what you are saying. And do you know what happens when you do that? At one point in time those poorest people, the only ones who are going to get social benefits, become like the RCMP officer with the turban. An intolerant, indifferent, uncaring, so-called majority says: "It is not in my best interest any more. I do not want to pay for it. And there sure as hell should not be a social program at all in this country".
That is precisely what is wrong with the Tory mentality. It is a mentality that invites Canadians to say that if you can find within your own financial means a way of looking after yourself, a way of providing for yourself and your family so that you do not need any additional assistance whatsoever, you do not want to participate in the social program. The logical extension is, Madam

Speaker, at the end of the day why should you pay in for social programs?

speechtext: You wouldn't know logic if it jumped up and hit you on the face.

My friend opposite states that I would not know logic if it jumped up and hit me on the face. I say to my friend opposite, that if this member opposite had the courage, had the integrity of a basic human being, this member opposite would not stand and applaud like a trained seal for a Prime Minister who has lied outright, repeatedly, to the people of Canada. That is the bottom line.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: Withdraw and apologize.

Madam Speaker, I understand that in parliamentary tradition I cannot use that word. So, for the sake of not having my speech interrupted by a trained, spineless seal, which is parliamentary, I want to withdraw the word "lied".

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext: And apologize.

Apologize? You want me to apologize to the senior citizens of Canada for a Prime Minister who committed to them that their social programs would not be touched and then robbed their pockets? I cannot apologize for the Prime Minister. He has to apologize for himself. You want me to apologize for a Prime Minister who brought his mother, a senior citizen, on a stage and said, "My mother is a senior citizen. I would no more abandon her than senior citizens of the country". I cannot apologize for that act of betrayal. That is up to the Prime Minister.
I am concerned that Canadians understand that what is at stake here today is not taking substantial dollars out of the pockets of some Canadians. What is at stake here today is whether or not we in this country are going to continue to have social programs universally available, and as a consequence, always available to those who need it the most. That is what is at stake.
For those who believe that in this Canada we ought not to emulate and try to replicate that nation to the south where it is dog eat dog, where it is a fact of life that you get the health care you can pay for; no more, no less; where it is perfectly acceptable to see your neighbour in the gutter as long as you have done all right and saved your pennies. For those who believe that a country like Canada, as large as it is, and as sparsely populated as it is, can only survive when citizenship has attached to it some common meaning no matter where you live and what
your circumstance, then we have to maintain our social programs.
This government, had it any idea that a nation's heartbeat, a nation's soul, a nation's conscience cannot be defined like pieces on a Monopoly board, it would withdraw this bill because for the few pennies the government is putting back in the Minister of Finance's coffers, it is ripping the heart and soul out of Canada. The government is asking us to become a nation of intolerant, indifferent, selfish, mean-spirited citizens. That is not in the fibre of this country. It will not be accepted by the people of Canada. Had this government the courage of its words and commitments, it would withdraw this bill.
The people of Canada will not forget this bloody betrayal of our basic values and beliefs by this government.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Questions or comments. The hon. member for York South-Weston.

Madam Speaker, I would like to put a question or two to my friend and colleague. I believe, as he does, that Canadians are fair-minded people, that they understand the need for the Government of Canada, indeed all governments, to tax in order to ensure certain programs and benefits and in order to improve the quality of life for all Canadians.
In so doing, I believe, and I am sure the member agrees, that any system of taxation has to be perceived to be fair to all Canadians, whether you are a rich stockbroker on Bay Street or a single mother or father on welfare in Metropolitan Toronto.
I would like to ask the member whether he really believes-and he has been in the House now for a considerable period of time-that this government over the last five years has been fair with its economic policies? The member has enunciated our concerns with respect to the so-called clawback provisions, the attempt to de-index senior citizen pensions. Can he indicate to me how this government could possibly conceive it or believe it to be fair to clawback seniorcitizen pensions on the one hand and to allow rich investors on Bay Street to claim capital gains? Where is the justice? Where is the fairness? Where is the equity in that type of economic policy?
